title: Estimation of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 COVID-19 Vaccine Effectiveness in Older US Veterans
abstract: Importance: The mRNA-1283 vaccine, a novel mRNA vaccine targeting immunodominant spike regions, was first used during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season. Older adults remain at elevated risk for severe COVID-19 outcomes, and clinical evidence of estimated vaccine effectiveness can inform seasonal vaccination policy. Objective: To compare the estimated effectiveness of mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccines against medically attended COVID-19 illness and COVID-19-associated hospitalization among US veterans aged 65 years or older. Design, Setting, and Participants: This was a retrospective matched cohort study emulating a target trial. US veterans aged 65 years or older who were enrolled in a national, integrated Veterans Health Administration (VHA) health care system and received an LP.8.1-formulated mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine between August 27, 2025, and January 31, 2026, were followed up for up to 150 days or through May 1, 2026. Exposure: Receipt of LP.8.1 mRNA-1283 or BNT162b2 vaccine. Main Outcome and Measures: The primary outcome was medically attended COVID-19 illness, defined by a positive SARS-CoV-2 test result linked to medical care or antiviral treatment or a primary COVID-19 diagnosis. Matching was performed on home county and calendar week of vaccination, followed by inverse probability of treatment weighting. Secondary outcomes included the individual component event of hospitalization. Measures were absolute and relative differences in 150-day cumulative incidence among patients receiving mRNA-1283 vs BNT162b2 vaccine, computed as the estimated relative vaccine effectiveness (rVE) percentage and absolute risk difference (ARD) per 10 000 persons, adjusted for demographic and clinical factors. Results: The cohort included 60 340 mRNA-1283 and 321 845 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (mean [SD] age, 76.8 [6.7] years; 94.2% male). Among the 294 499 participants in the final matched sample, medically attended COVID-19 occurred in 86 of 55 349 mRNA-1283 vaccine recipients (0.16%) and 672 of 239 150 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (0.28%), corresponding to estimated rVE of 35.9% (95% credible interval [CrI], 20.4%-49.7%) and an adjusted ARD of -10.0 (95% CrI, -14.3 to -5.6) events per 10 000 persons. COVID-19-associated hospitalization occurred in 11 mRNA-1283 vaccine recipients (0.02%) vs 114 BNT162b2 vaccine recipients (0.05%) (estimated rVE, 47.0% [95% CrI, 5.4%-74.8%]; adjusted ARD, -2.2 [95% CrI, -3.8 to -0.2] events per 10 000 persons). Conclusions and Relevance: In this cohort study of older US veterans during the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season, mRNA-1283 vaccination was associated with lower risks of medically attended COVID-19 outcomes and COVID-19 hospitalizations compared with BNT162b2 vaccination. The findings suggest that the mRNA-1283 vaccine may offer more clinically meaningful protection for older adults at high risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes and could inform seasonal vaccine selection.

title: Self-Reported Clinician Confidence in and Familiarity With Long COVID Care Following Continuing Medical Education Webinars: Unmatched Pre-Post Study.
abstract: Background An estimated 18-23 million Americans have had long COVID (LC), yet 54% and 72% of US physicians reported not being confident in diagnosing and treating LC, respectively. Continuing medical education (CME) is crucial to maintaining and improving clinical skills, and CME that incorporates need-based educational methods is associated with improved patient outcomes. Given limited clinician familiarity with LC, there is a need for an effective, widely accessible LC CME program. Objective This study assessed the effectiveness of 2 Stanford University-organized LC CME webinars, which aimed to provide comprehensive, up-to-date evaluation and management strategies through multidisciplinary didactic presentations and question-and-answer sessions. Methods Data from webinar attendees were collected through CME registration and prewebinar/postwebinar surveys. Registration surveys consisted of multiple-choice questions on profession, practice setting, experience treating vulnerable populations, and perception of LC. Prewebinar/postwebinar surveys consisted of multiple-choice questions on perception of LC, confidence in diagnosing LC, and familiarity with LC care. Prewebinar/postwebinar responses were compared using logistic regression, with Bonferroni adjustment to account for multiple testing. Statistical significance was defined as P Results The August 2024 webinar had 449 registrants: 48.6% (n=218) were physicians, and 29.0% (n=130) reported an affiliation with an academic medical center. title: Predictors of Long COVID in Adults With Untreated Mild-to-Moderate Coronavirus Disease 2019.
abstract: We evaluated risk factors for long COVID (LC) in the ACTIV-2/A5401 trial, with a focus on understanding the impact of sex. Findings were analyzed in nonhospitalized adults with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) receiving placebo within 10 days of symptoms. LC was defined as self-reporting COVID-19-related symptoms at study week 24 in a diary. Demographics and clinical variables, nasal viral RNA (vRNA), and inflammatory/coagulation markers were evaluated as predictors of LC, using modified Poisson regression models. Among 545 participants enrolled in January-August 2021 with a week 24 diary, the median age at entry was 44 years, 53% were female, 13% Black, 53% Hispanic/Latino, 83% US enrolled, 15% vaccinated, and 52% severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) seropositive. Seventy-four (14%) had LC (19% of female and 7% of male participants). Female sex was strongly associated with LC (adjusted risk ratio, 2.64 [95% confidence interval, 1.58-4.42]). Other predictors included US enrollment, higher total symptom score at entry, presence of symptoms at the end of the acute period (days 22-28), 28-day area under the curve of vRNA levels, and higher day 28 C-reactive protein and fibrinogen. The effect of sex persisted with adjustment for the other variables, and associations with symptoms and fibrinogen level varied by sex. In untreated adults with COVID-19, female sex, US enrollment, symptom and vRNA burden, and inflammatory/coagulation measures were associated with increased LC risk, with some associations varying by sex. The association with female sex was not significantly attenuated by adjustment for the assessed biomarkers. These data support sex-stratified investigations of LC, as well as a potential role of thromboinflammation. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04518410.

title: Changes in hepatic transaminases among children with COVID-19 in Najaf city Зміни рівня печінкових трансаміназ у дітей із COVID-19 у місті Наджаф
abstract: In December 2019, 54 cases of viral pneumonia of unknown cause emerged in Wuhan, China. The causative agent was later identified as a novel coronavirus producing severe acute respiratory syndrome, subsequently named SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19). The infection has since spread worldwide, affecting all age groups and causing multi-organ involvement. The purpose was to study changes in liver enzymes in relation to demographic variables, clinical course, and severity among hospitalized children with COVID-19. Materials and methods. This cross-sectional retrospective study included 50 confirmed pediatric COVID-19 cases aged 18 years or younger who were admitted to one of three hospitals in Najaf city after confirmation by real-time polymerase chain reaction from March 2020 to March 2021. Cases were classified as mild-to-moderate or severe according to the seventh trial version of the National Health Commission program. Demographic data, history, physical findings, and investigations were collected from all patients’ files. Liver function tests were recorded for all children. Associations between the clinical and demographic variables and liver enzyme levels were examined using bivariate tests only. No a priori sample size calculation was performed, and no multivariable modelling was undertaken, so the analysis is exploratory. Among the 50 confirmed cases, severe disease was found in 21 patients (42 %), whereas 29 (58 %) had mild-to-moderate course. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) were analyzed in relation to the clinical variables. Mean ALT and AST were higher in severe than in mild-to-moderate disease (p = 0.001 and p = 0.05, respectively) and in children who died than in those whose illness resolved (p < 0.001 and p = 0.013, respectively). Both enzymes positively correlated with length of stay (r = 0.54 for ALT and r = 0.23 for AST). ALP was not associated with severity (p = 0.556), length of stay, or outcome (p = 0.745). All estimates are unadjusted. In this retrospective study, higher ALT and AST levels were associated with more severe disease and a fatal outcome. Because the design is cross-sectional and the estimates are unadjusted, these findings describe associations only and do not establish that COVID-19 caused the enzyme changes. Severe disease was seen in every age group. Both toddlers in the sample had severe illness, but two children are far too few to support any conclusion about age-specific risk. The study should be read as exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

title: Predictors of High-Flow Nasal Oxygen Success in COVID-19 Respiratory Failure: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Study
abstract: There is no clear consensus regarding optimal use of oxygen therapy for patients with type 1 respiratory failure secondary to COVID-19. This retrospective observational cohort study evaluates high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) delivery in adults with COVID-19 and compares potential predictors of treatment success. Adults receiving HFNO in two tertiary hospitals in Hull, UK, between 1 March 2020 and 1 March 2021 were included. Demographic, clinical, and biochemical data were extracted from hospital records; prognostic scores were calculated retrospectively. HFNO success was defined as an improvement in oxygenation with subsequent discontinuation of HFNO without escalation to non-invasive or mechanical ventilation, or death. In total, 108 patients received HFNO (mean age 64.1 years; 66% male; 94% White/White British). Of the 65% (70/108) considered suitable for ICU, 59% (41/70) achieved HFNO success. Among patients not suitable for ICU (38/108), 24% (9/38) achieved HFNO success. Multivariate analysis identified older age (adjusted OR 1.049, 95% CI 1.015–1.085; p = 0.005) and higher CRP (adjusted OR 1.007, 95% CI 1.002–1.011; p = 0.003) as independent predictors of HFNO failure. The ISARIC 4C score demonstrated 70% positive and 71% negative predictive value for HFNO success (AUROC 0.726, 95% CI 0.628–0.823). These factors may help guide appropriate use of HFNO in patients with COVID-19.

source_records.abstract: There is no clear consensus regarding optimal use of oxygen therapy for patients with type 1 respiratory failure secondary to COVID-19. This retrospective observational cohort study evaluates high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) delivery in adults with COVID-19 and compares potential predictors of treatment success. Adults receiving HFNO in two tertiary hospitals in Hull, UK, between 1 March 2020 and 1 March 2021 were included. Demographic, clinical, and biochemical data were extracted from hospital records; prognostic scores were calculated retrospectively. HFNO success was defined as an improvement in oxygenation with subsequent discontinuation of HFNO without escalation to non-invasive or mechanical ventilation, or death. In total, 108 patients received HFNO (mean age 64.1 years; 66% male; 94% White/White British). Of the 65% (70/108) considered suitable for ICU, 59% (41/70) achieved HFNO success. Among patients not suitable for ICU (38/108), 24% (9/38) achieved HFNO success. Multivariate analysis identified older age (adjusted OR 1.049, 95% CI 1.015–1.085; p = 0.005) and higher CRP (adjusted OR 1.007, 95% CI 1.002–1.011; p = 0.003) as independent predictors of HFNO failure. The ISARIC 4C score demonstrated 70% positive and 71% negative predictive value for HFNO success (AUROC 0.726, 95% CI 0.628–0.823). These factors may help guide appropriate use of HFNO in patients with COVID-19.

title: Conservative Protestantism and Elevated COVID-19 Mortality in the U.S.
abstract: Background: Conservative Protestant communities have exhibited various COVID-19 risks, including some evidence of elevated pandemic mortality, and have long had a lackluster overall mortality track record. Are there distinct patterns of conservative Protestant COVID-19 mortality within U.S. Building on previous religion and COVID-19 research, along with insights from religious ecology and social network theories, we hypothesize that counties with greater proportions of denominational conservative Protestants (i.e., evangelicals, fundamentalists, and Pentecostals combined) will exhibit significantly higher mortality rates than those in which other religious groups and the non-religious have a more substantial market share. We further anticipate that counties populated by larger proportions of nondenominational conservative Protestants will not be subject to the same COVID-19 mortality risks because these groups exhibit network fragmentation, whereby they are outside the conservative denominational orbit. Methods: Data for this study come from multiple sources. COVID-19 mortality data were drawn from the New York Times COVID Tracking Project, 2021, and are supplemented with CDC data when needed. County-level religious market share was obtained from the 2020 U.S. Religion Census via the ARDA. Sociodemographic controls were taken from County Health Rankings, 2023, which integrates U.S. Census, ACS, NCHS, and AHRF data. County-level presidential election results were sourced from the MIT Election Data Science Lab. The final analytic sample includes 3032 counties with complete data. Results: Our findings reveal significantly higher rates of COVID-19 mortality in counties with a greater share of denominational conservative Protestant adherents, net of controls. We find similar fatality rates for counties populated by different conservative Protestant subgroups (evangelical, fundamentalist, and Pentecostal adherents). Additionally, some evidence of reduced COVID-19 mortality in counties with greater concentrations of fragmented (mostly nondenominational) conservative Protestants was observed. No significant association was observed for counties with greater isolationist conservative Protestant (Amish and Mennonite) market shares. Conclusion: The social ecology of religion proves to be an important determinant of public health in the form of COVID-19 mortality. Our findings have direct implications for ongoing research and practice concerning religion, health, and longevity.

title: Asthma prevalence and influenza and COVID-19 vaccination coverage among children aged ≤17 years with asthma.
abstract: Objective Children with asthma are at increased risk for complications from respiratory infectious diseases. This study assessed asthma prevalence and influenza and COVID-19 vaccination coverage among children with asthma. Methods Data from the 2024 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) were analyzed to assess asthma prevalence and influenza and COVID-19 vaccination coverage by asthma status among children. Results Current asthma prevalence was 6.5% among children aged ≤17 years. Prevalence was higher among children aged 5-12 years (8.2%) and 13-17 years (7.8%) compared with those aged Conclusion Asthma prevalence was higher among older children, males, and non-Hispanic Black children. Influenza and COVID-19 vaccination coverage among children with asthma remained low. Tailored strategies are needed to reduce the asthma burden and improve vaccination coverage in populations with lower uptake.

title: Multi-omics signatures indicative of status and effectiveness of vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 in ferrets
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic prompted one of the most rapid vaccination efforts in history in an attempt to mitigate the global health and socio-economic burden of the disease. Today, the challenge remains in maintaining vaccine efficacy given the continuous evolution of key antigenic sites in the viral Spike protein. Access to multi-omics data analysis and machine learning (ML) approaches has greatly enhanced our ability to evaluate biomarkers associated with diagnosis, prognosis, drug discovery, and therapeutics, and can be used to obtain additional insights from traditional efficacy studies. In this study, multi-omics data (transcriptomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, proteomics) were processed from 16 ferrets vaccinated with DNA vaccines based on Wuhan-Hu-1 and SynCon spike sequences. Multi-omics data was integrated into Random Forest models to identify potential biomarkers indicative of vaccination status and the development of neutralising antibody titres against six SARS-CoV-2 variants. Causal analysis, based on Empirical Bayes Matrix Factorisation, was used to identify biological processes occurring between vaccination and a positive immune response. Several putative transcriptomic, lipid and metabolite biomarkers associated with reducing hyper-inflammation and maintaining cell homeostasis were identified using Random Forest models incorporating the omics analyses. These were similarly found when using vaccine immune response as class labels. Additionally, causal analysis identified four and three latent factors associated with vaccination status and response, respectively. Within these, several enriched gene sets relating to cell function and regulation, including ATP-synthesis and mitochondrial related processes were identified. Other genes also included those with secondary immune functions, particularly relating to chemokine and cytokines. This study provides a holistic analysis of ferret immune response to SARS-CoV-2 by integrating multi-omics data with ML and casual analysis and potential targets for further investigation.

title: AlphaScreen profiling of extracellular vesicle-associated platelet, immune, and vascular markers reveals disease-specific signatures in ME/CFS, fibromyalgia, and long COVID
abstract: Introduction: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), fibromyalgia (FM), and long COVID (LC-19) are chronic diseases with overlapping clinical features and poorly understood pathophysiology. Increasing evidence suggests the involvement of immune dysregulation, endothelial dysfunction, and altered vascular physiology. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are key mediators of intercellular communication and are envisioned as sensors of homeostasis and disease. The aim of this study was to determine whether EV marker profiling could provide a basis for the differential diagnosis of ME/CFS, FM and LC-19 and/or patient stratification. Methods: EV-enriched plasma from ME/CFS, FM, cases co-diagnosed with ME/CFS and FM, LC-19 patients, and matched healthy controls (n = 10 per study group) were analyzed. EV concentration and size distribution were assessed by nanoparticle tracking analysis, followed by targeted profiling of EV-associated surface markers via AlphaScreen, including tetraspanins CD9 and CD63, platelet- (CD41/CD61), myeloid- (CD13), immune- (CD74 and CX3CR1), and renin-angiotensin system- associated ACE1 (also known as CD143), and ACE2 surface markers. Results: The studied disease groups presented distinct EV signatures. LC-19 samples exhibited the most pronounced and coordinated alterations, characterized by increased levels of CD9/CD74, CD9/CX3CR1, and CD9/ACE1-positive EVs, along with reduced overall particle concentrations. Notably, platelet-derived CD9/CD41/CD61-positive EVs were significantly elevated in both LC-19 and ME/CFS, as compared to healthy controls, indicating enhanced platelet activation. Immune-associated markers revealed differential pathway activation in LC-19, with CD74-positive EVs reflecting antigen presentation and inflammatory signaling, and CX3CR1-positive EVs indicating altered leukocyte trafficking and vascular interaction. Increased ACE1-positive EVs in LC-19 further suggested a shift toward pro-inflammatory renin-angiotensin signaling. Conclusion: Collectively, these findings support a disease-specific dysregulation of platelet, immune, and vascular pathways. The integrated EV signatures distinguish LC-19 from the related chronic conditions ME/CFS and FM, highlighting the potential of EV-based profiling for differential diagnosis. Our results provide a systems-level perspective on the differential pathophysiology of these disorders and identify EV-associated markers as candidate biomarkers with clinical value.

title: Antibiotic drug prescription in the outpatient paediatric population of the Lombardy region before and after the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the trend in antibiotic prescriptions in the paediatric population of the Italian Lombardy region before and after the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods: Antibiotic prescriptions dispensed to subjects under 18 years old in the Italian Lombardy Region from 2014 to 2024 were analysed. Antibiotic prevalence rates and prescription rates, the proportion of drugs belonging to the Access group of WHO classification, and the amoxicillin index were calculated for calendar year, age groups, and local health units (LHU). Results: The prevalence of antibiotic prescriptions decreased between 2014 and 2019 (from 40.4% to 36.4%), with a further drop in the pandemic period, followed by an increase between 2022 and 2024 (from 30.9% to 38.1%). No differences were found when comparing the percentage of Access antibiotics (61.1% vs. 60.9%) or the amoxicillin index (17.1% vs. 17.2%) in 2024 versus 2014. In 2024, the prevalence ranged from 36.3% to 41.7% at the LHU level. The percentage of Access antibiotics ranged from 55.5% to 64.8%, and the amoxicillin index from 11.6% to 26.3%. Compared to infants, adolescents had the lowest probability of receiving Access antibiotics (OR: 0.29; 95%CI: 0.28–0.30) and amoxicillin (OR: 0.14; 95%CI: 0.13–0.14). Conclusions: During the pandemic, there was a decrease in antibiotic prescriptions, with a rebound after the lifting of containment measures. No changes were observed in quality indicators, but the heterogeneity observed among geographical settings suggests that improvements are needed and that interventions should be adapted to local settings

title: Neuroinflammation as a Mechanism in Long COVID
abstract: Long COVID is recognized as a chronic post-viral condition characterized by fatigue, cognitive impairment, mood changes, and other neuropsychiatric symptoms that go beyond the acute phase of COVID-19. More research is now suggesting that neuroinflammation processes, involving microglial reactivity, altered cytokine signaling, and increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier, may contribute to the persistence of these symptoms. This paper provides a critical review of four recent empirical studies that directly examined neuroinflammatory mechanisms in individuals with long COVID using functional neuroimaging, biomarker analysis, and structural MRI measures. Across studies, converging evidence shows persistent central and peripheral immune activation linked to deficits in memory, attention, and mood regulation. Despite promising findings, the literature is limited by small sample sizes, inconsistent diagnostic criteria, and primarily cross-sectional designs, which limit conclusions about causality. Differences in imaging techniques and biomarker measurement approaches hinder direct comparison and synthesis of results. Future research should prioritize longitudinal, multimodal designs that integrate neuroimaging with immune and behavioral markers to clarify the trajectory and clinical relevance of neuroinflammation in long COVID. Overall, the evidence suggests that neuroinflammation plays a significant role in long COVID related cognitive and mood disturbances and emphasizes the need for biologically guided and consistent clinical approaches.

source_records.abstract: Long COVID is recognized as a chronic post-viral condition characterized by fatigue, cognitive impairment, mood changes, and other neuropsychiatric symptoms that go beyond the acute phase of COVID-19. More research is now suggesting that neuroinflammation processes, involving microglial reactivity, altered cytokine signaling, and increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier, may contribute to the persistence of these symptoms. This paper provides a critical review of four recent empirical studies that directly examined neuroinflammatory mechanisms in individuals with long COVID using functional neuroimaging, biomarker analysis, and structural MRI measures. Across studies, converging evidence shows persistent central and peripheral immune activation linked to deficits in memory, attention, and mood regulation. Despite promising findings, the literature is limited by small sample sizes, inconsistent diagnostic criteria, and primarily cross-sectional designs, which limit conclusions about causality. Differences in imaging techniques and biomarker measurement approaches hinder direct comparison and synthesis of results. Future research should prioritize longitudinal, multimodal designs that integrate neuroimaging with immune and behavioral markers to clarify the trajectory and clinical relevance of neuroinflammation in long COVID. Overall, the evidence suggests that neuroinflammation plays a significant role in long COVID related cognitive and mood disturbances and emphasizes the need for biologically guided and consistent clinical approaches.
source_records.journal: Journal of Clinical Psychology and Neurology

title: Comparative analysis of the development of oral language as a cognitive process constitutive of learning in child cohorts exposed to COVID-19 lockdown
abstract: This study analyzes oral language development as a constitutive cognitive process of learning in child cohorts exposed to COVID-19 confinement. A mixed-method, comparative, and correlational approach is proposed with a sample of 60 children distributed across three cohorts: pre-, during-, and post-pandemic. Exposure to the pandemic context is examined through questionnaires and interviews with parents and caregivers, while language development is assessed through PLON-R, systematic observation, and pedagogical records. The theoretical review and available contextual evidence suggest variations in morphosyntactic, semantic, and pragmatic performance associated with reduced social interaction, disrupted routines, and lower communicative stimulation. The study provides an analytical basis for understanding the relationship among confinement, language, and learning, and for supporting educational and psychopedagogical interventions in post-pandemic contexts.
journal: Journal of Systems and Educational Management

title: Epidemic waves and cytokine signatures of seven respiratory pathogens after COVID-19 restrictions
abstract: Background: Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) during COVID-19 created population-level immunity debt. Following NPI lifting in China (May 2023), clinicians face unprecedented resurgence patterns of respiratory pathogens with altered age distributions and co-infection dynamics, but comprehensive comparative cytokine profiling across diverse pathogens remains limited. Methods: We conducted a 20-month prospective-retrospective surveillance study (June 2024-January 2026) of 54,902 febrile patients, with nested cytokine profiling (n=187) across 11 groups using a 47-analyte multiplex panel. Random forest machine learning with 10-fold stratified cross-validation identified optimal cytokine panels for pathogen discrimination. Results: Three sequential epidemic waves emerged: Wave 1 (July-August 2024, SARS-CoV-2, n=1,988), Wave 2 (December 2024-March 2025, IAV, n=5,373), and Wave 3 (November 2025-January 2026, IAV+HRV, n=8,567). The 9.5% co-infection rate (2,986 cases) fell within the upper pre-pandemic range. G-CSF and IL-1Ra were universally elevated across all pathogens (1.4- to 100.2-fold and 1.8- to 41.7-fold vs. healthy controls, respectively), serving as broad inflammatory markers. Machine learning classification using five cytokines (MIF, IP-10, RANTES, G-CSF, IL-1Ra) achieved 87.3% cross-validated accuracy (95% CI 82.1-92.4%) for pathogen-group discrimination. IAV exhibited a unique IL-4-dominant profile (105.8-fold elevation, η2=0.84), while MP demonstrated distinct immune suppression (IL-16 and PDGF-BB suppressed 0.5-fold). Co-infections generated supra-additive cytokine amplification (e.g., MIG 36.6-fold in HRV+MP vs. 4.2- to 7.3-fold in single infections) and dysregulated IL-10 anti-inflammatory feedback. Conclusions: Pathogen-specific cytokine signatures enable rapid etiological inference from single plasma samples. G-CSF and IL-1Ra serve as universal ARI screening markers, while IAV-specific IL-4 elevation and MP-specific immune suppression offer diagnostic and therapeutic targets for precision medicine in respiratory infectious diseases.

title: SARS-CoV-2 spike and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors: a testable context-dependent hypothesis across acute and post-acute disease
abstract: Studies of SARS-CoV-2 spike and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) have reported negative binding results, positive or mixed electrophysiological findings, and reduced receptor surface expression. These observations do not constitute a demonstrated discrepancy in binding affinity. We examine whether three measurable dimensions can explain part of the disagreement: the molecular preparation, receptor mechanism, and timing and compartment of exposure. The central hypothesis is that processing or redistribution of spike may alter the opportunity for nicotinic modulation and that appropriately located, active material could contribute to symptoms in a subset of post-acute disease. No study has demonstrated the complete pathway from spike processing through receptor-active human exposure to a clinical phenotype. Negative α7 experiments included isolated peptides and S1, so cleavage or S1 release cannot be assumed sufficient for activity. The S2-associated surface-expression mechanism requires intracellular co-expression and is distinct from extracellular S1 pharmacology. Antigen detection is treated as a reason to investigate exposure, not evidence of receptor occupancy. We separate experimental observations, mechanistic interpretations and clinical hypotheses, and specify results that would reject individual branches. A minimal programme would first test matched preparations, then establish receptor-specific activity of patient material at measured exposure, and only then examine longitudinal clinical relationships. ACE2/renin–angiotensin signalling and other disease mechanisms remain alternatives or potential interacting pathways. Overlapping symptoms after infection and vaccination justify comparison but do not establish an identical cause. This framework makes the proposed contribution of spike to nicotinic dysfunction testable without presenting it as a general explanation of COVID-19 or a basis for treatment.

title: Protecting vulnerable children: parental drivers of COVID-19 vaccine uptake in children with pediatric cancers
abstract: Children with pediatric cancers are especially vulnerable to COVID-19, yet vaccination rates among this population have remained suboptimal. Understanding what shapes parental decision-making about vaccinating their immunocompromised children is critical for improving uptake. We examined the extent to which COVID-19 vaccine uptake among children with cancer is predicted by demographic characteristics, general vaccine hesitancy, and specific Health Belief Model (HBM) constructs. In early 2022, 125 parents of children with pediatric cancers in active treatment completed a survey. Measures included demographics, the Parent Attitudes about Childhood Vaccines scale, and COVID-19 specific HBM constructs. Hierarchical logistic regression identified predictors of vaccine uptake. 51.2% of children had received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose. Mothers were less likely than fathers to have vaccinated their child. Contrary to expectations, general vaccine hesitancy did not predict uptake. However, HBM constructs higher perceived benefits, greater perceived severity of COVID-19, and greater self-efficacy were linked with increased COVID-19 vaccine uptake. Parental decisions to vaccinate their children with cancer were best explained by COVID-19 vaccine-specific beliefs, not general vaccine hesitancy. Interventions as well as future pandemic preparedness plans should emphasize vaccine benefits and disease severity, with pediatric oncology health care providers playing a key role in communication.

title: Perceived therapeutic benefits and adverse effects of COVIDEX among covid-19 patients in Uganda: A cross-sectional study
abstract: During the second wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in Uganda, health system constraints led many patients to seek alternative and supportive therapies, including herbal medicines.COVIDEX®, a locally developed herbal product, was widely used following emergency authorization despite the absence of formal clinical trial data.This study assessed self-reported outcomes and adverse effects associated with COVIDEX® use among patients with COVID-19 in Uganda.A cross-sectional online survey was conducted between 3 and 17 July 2021 using a public reporting tool developed and posted online by the Pharmaceutical Society of Uganda.Respondents included patients, caregivers, and healthcare providers who provided information on COVIDEX® use, disease severity, concurrent treatments, perceived time to improvement, outcomes, and adverse events.Data collected by the Pharmaceutical Society of Uganda and provided in-kind to the research team were analyzed descriptively using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) version 25.A total of 222 complete responses were analyzed.Most reports concerned male patients (54.9%), with a mean age of 24.2 ± 13.3 years.Among the reported cases, 82.9% had laboratory-confirmed COVID-19.Disease severity was reported as moderate in 50.5% of cases, mild in 28.8%, severe in 18.5%, and critical in 2.3%.The mean reported time to perceived improvement following COVIDEX® administration was 39.9 ± 12.4 years.Overall, 96.3% of patients were reported to have improved, including 73.6% who reportedly achieved full recovery, while three deaths (1.4%) were reported.Adverse events were reported by 34.2% of respondents and were generally mild and selflimiting.Survey respondents reported rapid perceived improvement and a low frequency of predominantly mild adverse effects following COVIDEX® use.Given the observational and self-reported nature of these findings, controlled clinical studies are required to establish the safety and efficacy of COVIDEX®.
journal: African Journal of Pharmacy and Pharmacology

title: Newly Diagnosed Oral Cancer Stage and Time from Diagnosis to Treatment in the Pre-COVID-19 and Early COVID-19 Periods: A Nationwide Cohort Study
abstract: Background: During the COVID-19 pandemic, patients’ willingness to seek medical attention decreased. Patients with precancerous lesions may have missed out on opportunities for early detection. This affected the time to the initiation of treatment for patients with oral cancer. This study examined whether patients with oral cancer were less likely to be at early cancer stages and analyzed whether the time from the diagnosis to the initiation of treatment was delayed during the pandemic. Methods: This retrospective study analyzed data from the Taiwan National Health Insurance Research Database, Cancer Registry File, and Multiple Cause of Death File. Patients who received new diagnoses of oral cancer were divided into a pre-COVID-19 group (2018) and an early COVID-19 group (2020). Propensity score matching was performed between the two cohorts. Conditional logistic regression analyses were conducted to evaluate the risks of an early-stage oral cancer diagnosis and treatment delay from diagnosis to treatment initiation in the two periods. Results: The odds ratio (OR) for early cancer staging among patients with oral cancer in the early COVID-19 period was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.82–0.96) compared to the pre-COVID-19 period. The OR for delayed treatment among patients with oral cancer in the early COVID-19 period compared with that in the pre-COVID-19 period was 0.95 (95% CI: 0.86–1.05; p = 0.337). Conclusions: The early COVID-19 period was associated with a higher risk of advanced cancer staging, and we did not find a significant association with a delay in the initiation of treatment among patients with oral cancer in Taiwan.

title: Health choices in transition: a systematic review and meta-analysis of self-medication in India across diverse populations and locations before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Self-medication is a growing public health concern, especially in low- and middle-income countries like India. Despite its widespread practice, a comprehensive national-level synthesis of the prevalence and demographic patterns of self-medication in India has been lacking. This systematic review examines that gap by assessing self-medication prevalence across diverse populations, states, regions, and time periods in India. A systematic search was conducted across three major databases—PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science—to identify peer-reviewed articles on self-medication in India. Studies were screened for eligibility using the PRISMA 2020 Statement, and a total of 145 studies comprising 69,876 participants were included in the meta-analysis. The quality assessments of the included articles were conducted using the JBI checklist for critical appraisal. The pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects models. title: COVID-19 Vaccination Status and Attitudes Towards Vaccination in Pregnant and Breastfeeding Mothers
abstract: Aim: The short- and long-term side effects of vaccines developed against COVID-19 and the uncertainty of their protective effects affect the attitudes of pregnant and breastfeeding women towards vaccination. This study aimed to investigate the COVID-19 vaccination status of pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, their attitudes towards the vaccine, and the factors influencing these attitudes.Materials and Methods: This descriptive and cross-sectional study was conducted with 322 pregnant and breastfeeding mothers who applied to the obstetrics and gynecology outpatient clinic of a training and research hospital in Izmir between August 2022 and February 2023. Data were collected via face-to-face interviews using the Individual Identification Form and the Attitudes Towards COVID-19 Vaccine Scale. Descriptive statistics, Kruskal-Wallis, and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for data analysis.Results: It was determined that 75.2% of pregnant and breastfeeding mothers had received the COVID-19 vaccine. The mean score of the Positive Attitude subdimension of the Attitudes Towards COVID-19 Vaccine Scale was 2.85 ± 1.00, while the mean score of the Negative Attitude subdimension was 3.04 ± 0.71. There was a weak positive correlation between the mean age of women (r = 0.138; p = 0.013) and their spouses (r = 0.160; p = 0.004) and the Positive Attitude subdimension scores. A statistically significant difference was also found in the Positive Attitude subdimension scores according to the parity (KW = 10.676; p = 0.014), with women who had four or more pregnancies showing more positive attitudes.Conclusions: Pregnant and breastfeeding mothers were found to have a generally positive attitude towards COVID-19 vaccination. In vaccine studies that may emerge in future pandemics, policy makers, public authorities, and health professionals should work collaboratively for such special groups, and vaccination strategies, counseling, and educational interventions that take individual differences into account should be planned.

title: [Quality of practical nursing education during a crisis: A qualitative study involving students, clinical supervisors, and teachers, focusing on 'lessons learned' from the Covid-19 pandemic].
abstract: Background There is currently a growing focus on national and international discussions regarding the review of the Covid-19 pandemic, with a view to better managing future crises. Whilst the pressures faced by healthcare professionals during the pandemic are well documented, the situation of nursing students has yet to be properly examined in Germany. The aim of the study was to analyze the situation in nursing practice during the pandemic and to identify starting points for a better preparedness for future crises. Method Six retrospective focus groups (April to June 2023) were conducted with nursing students, clinical supervisors, and nursing teachers on their experiences and the quality of practical nursing education in Germany during the pandemic. The data were evaluated using deductive qualitative content analysis along the quality dimensions of structural framework conditions, education processes, and learning outcomes. Further categories were created inductively. Results The education environment was significantly restricted due to staff shortages. Nursing students were frequently deployed to make up for the staff shortages. Structured education and training processes could only be implemented to a limited extent. The organizations responsible for practical education applied inconsistent criteria regarding the extent to which students were involved in caring for patients who had tested positive for Covid-19. Some students were exposed to high levels of physical and psychological stress. Competence deficits caused by the pandemic were compensated for by individualized learning opportunities provided by schools and practice settings. Discussion During the pandemic, practical nursing education was not structurally secured as a core function within the healthcare system and took a back seat to care requirements. The responsibilities assigned to nursing students were defined according to the specific institution; however, the students were overwhelmed at times, and psychosocial support services, in particular, would have been necessary. Conclusion To prepare for future crises, binding and nuanced regulations tailored to students' levels of education are required regarding the deployment and responsible involvement of students in crisis situations. Students must receive continuous psychosocial support during crisis-related deployments. Curricula and training plans should prepare nursing students for crises across all learning settings, and following the initial emergency measures, appropriately qualified staff should pursue the specific education and training objectives.

title: MiR-223 and miR-323 as biomarkers of inflammatory and neuropsychiatric alterations in long COVID with chronic viral hepatitis.
abstract: Long COVID involves persistent physical, mental, and functional symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Its biological mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly with chronic viral hepatitis. This study investigated associations between microRNA (miRNA) expression and mental and physical health outcomes in individuals with Long COVID, considering chronic hepatitis B or C. This cross-sectional study included 80 individuals divided into four groups (n = 20 each): Long COVID, chronic viral hepatitis, Long COVID with hepatitis, and controls. Depression, anxiety, quality of life, fatigue, and functional status were assessed using validated scales, including the Post-COVID Functional Status Scale. Expression of miR-122, miR-143, miR-223, and miR-323 was quantified by RT-qPCR. Associations were evaluated using non-parametric tests and correlation analyses. MiR-143, miR-223, and miR-323 were significantly upregulated in individuals with Long COVID and hepatitis. MiRNA expression was associated with mental and physical health outcomes, particularly through a positive correlation between miR-323 expression and anxiety levels in individuals with Long COVID and hepatitis. MiR-223 was the only miRNA significantly overexpressed in this group compared with all other groups, suggesting its potential as a biomarker of coexisting conditions. Depression and anxiety affected up to 75% and 50% of individuals in the Long COVID groups, respectively (p < 0.05).These findings suggest that circulating miRNAs, particularly miR-223, miR-143, and miR-323, are associated with Long COVID in the presence of chronic viral hepatitis and may serve as biomarkers of disease burden and clinical heterogeneity.

title: Doggybone DNA vaccine provides long lasting immunity against SARS CoV 2 than Covaxin
abstract: Durable and balanced immune responses are critical for effectual SARS-CoV-2 vaccination. We compared the immunogenicity of a novel linear doggybone DNA vaccine encoding the full length membrane anchored spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (S-dbDNA) with that of a licensed inactivated whole-virion vaccine, Covaxin, in a murine model. S-dbDNA induced significantly higher anti-S1 IgG titres with strong reactivity to the RBD (receptor-binding domain) and superior neutralization of virulent SARS-CoV-2. S-dbDNA also elicited higher frequencies of mono- and polyfunctional CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, along with cytokine-producing NK and NKT cells, compared with Covaxin. Importantly, S-dbDNA generated more durable immune memory, with sustained antibody, neutralization, and T-cell responses detectable up to 120 days post-immunization. These findings support linear DNA vaccines as a promising platform for SARS-CoV-2 and emerging pathogens.

title: [2026-11-12] Quarantine Experiences of People at Risk of COVID-19: A Qualitative Study
abstract: Background: COVID-19 is an emerging infectious disease that has affected people’s daily lives. Self-quarantine is an important public health measure for preventing the transmission of COVID-19 among individuals at risk of infection. Understanding individuals’ experiences during quarantine may help inform effective support strategies and improve adherence to public health measures. Objective: To explore the self-quarantine experiences of COVID-19 high-risk individuals and their views on Thailand’s pandemic situation. Methods: A descriptive qualitative design was employed. Fifteen participants who underwent self-quarantine were purposively recruited from outpatients at acute respiratory infection clinics. Data were collected through in-depth interviews conducted from May 2020 to June 2020 and analyzed using content analysis. Trustworthiness was established through triangulation. Results: Four main themes emerged from the self-quarantine experiences: 1) positive definition of quarantine, 2) adapting to a new way of life, 3) impact of quarantine, and 4) support system during quarantine. Multisectoral collaboration, family support, and community support were identified as important for promoting adherence to public health measure during self-quarantine. Participants also emphasized the need for timely, clear, and adequate communication regarding COVID-19 outbreaks, disease severity, prevention and control measures, and the status of the pandemic. Conclusions: These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive support and effective risk communication during self-quarantine. Providing timely and accurate information and strengthening support from family, community and relevant sectors may help shape community attitudes and reduce stigma and discrimination toward individuals undergoing quarantine.

title: A randomized controlled trial of an intravenous SARS-CoV-2 protease inhibitor PF-07304814 for hospitalized COVID-19 patients
abstract: Abstract Background Antiviral treatment options for hospitalized COVID-19 patients are limited. Methods We conducted a phase 2/3, randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial of PF-07304814, an intravenous SARS-CoV-2 protease inhibitor. From September-December 2021, adults hospitalized for COVID-19 were randomized to continuous intravenous infusion of PF-07304814 (250 mg/24 hours) or placebo for 120-hours (or hospital discharge). The primary outcome was time to sustained recovery through day 90. The primary safety outcome through day 28 was a composite of death, serious adverse events, organ failure, thromboembolic events (pre-specified as events of special interest), serious infections, and grade 3/4 adverse events. Results We randomized 58 participants (32 PF-07304814; 26 placebo). After three participants experienced serious adverse events (SAEs), two related to thromboembolic events and one to acute abdominal pain, the trial was put on hold by regulators and thereafter administratively closed. The composite safety outcome through day 28 occurred in 17/32 (53%) participants assigned PF-07304814 and 11/26 (42%) participants assigned placebo (hazard ratio (HR) 1.20, 95% CI 0.56–2.57; p = 0.64). The estimated cumulative incidence of sustained recovery at day 90 was 75% for PF-07304814 and 50% for placebo participants (sHR 1.41; 95% CI: 0.71–2.80). In the PF-07304814 arm, 4 (12.5%) experienced a thromboembolic event; all died by day 90. In the placebo arm, 2 (7.7%) experienced a thromboembolic event (HR 1.46, 95% CI 0.27–7.95); both survived to the end of follow-up. Conclusion The risk/benefit of PF-07304814 could not be established due to early termination of enrollment. Rates of thromboembolic events with PF-07304814 were not statistically different than placebo. Trial Registration TICO ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04501978, Registration date: August 6, 2020. Keypoints The safety and efficacy of an intravenous SARS-CoV-2 protease inhibitor PF-07304814 could not be established in this randomized controlled trial of 58 participants. These results provide preliminary data for testing other protease inhibitors and antiviral medications in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

The safety and efficacy of an intravenous SARS-CoV-2 protease inhibitor PF-07304814 could not be established in this randomized controlled trial of 58 participants. These results provide preliminary data for testing other protease inhibitors and antiviral medications in hospitalized COVID-19 patients.

title: Federated Learning for Cross-Regional Epidemic Forecasting with Asynchronous Outbreaks
abstract: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.

title: CONFIDENT: A Randomized Trial to Increase COVID-19 Vaccine Confidence in Long-Term Care Workers
abstract: Background: In 2021, nursing homes were at the forefront of the COVID-19 pandemic, with resident deaths occurring at over 100 times the rate in the general population. Long-term care workers (LTCWs), who care for vulnerable older adults and are an at-risk population themselves, are known to be a COVID-19 vaccine-hesitant population. However, vaccination protects against the severe effects of COVID-19. This study was organized to understand the effectiveness of 2 interventions intended to increase LTCWs’ confidence in, and uptake of, the COVID-19 vaccines, with the goal to protect their health and the health of the residents served. Objectives: This study had 3 aims: (1) compare the impact of 2 online interventions (dialogue-based webinar [“webinar”] and social media website [“social site”]) to enhanced usual practice (“usual practice”—the COVID-19 vaccine content on the website of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) on COVID-19 vaccine confidence and other outcomes;(2) determine if LTCWs’ characteristics mediate or moderate the interventions’ impact on outcomes; and (3) explore the delivery contexts, characteristics, and processes needed to sustain use of the interventions. Methods: We conducted a hybrid effectiveness-implementation type 2 study with a continuous participatory approach. We evaluated intervention effectiveness in a 3-arm randomized controlled trial (RCT) (aims 1 and 2). We explored intervention implementation (aim 3) through intervention co-design, a process evaluation, and a post-trial sustainability phase. For the RCT, between May 2022 and January 2023, we recruited LTCWs 18 years and older who lived in the United States and had not received a COVID-19 booster vaccine and/or were at least somewhat worried about the vaccines. We recruited participants through social media posts and advertisements, an email listserv, and in person at long-term care (LTC) facilities. Participants completed a baseline eligibility and enrollment survey before being randomly assigned. Participants were sent 3 follow-up surveys to assess primary and secondary outcomes 3 weeks, 3 months, and 6 months after baseline. For aim 1, the primary outcome assessed at 3 weeks postbaseline was COVID-19 vaccine confidence, which was defined as a person’s belief in the importance, safety, and effectiveness of the COVID-19 vaccine. Secondary outcomes assessed at all time points included COVID-19 vaccine and booster uptake and intent, net promoter scores, whether participants felt informed about the vaccines, their identification of vaccine information and misinformation (knowledge), and trust in information provided by different sources. For aim 2, we explored whether some secondary outcomes (feeling informed, knowledge, and trust) mediated the relationship between trial arms and vaccine confidence. We also explored heterogeneity of treatment effects for baseline vaccination and booster status, religious beliefs, perceived influence of others, age, race and ethnicity, personal experiences with COVID-19, education, LTCW role, duration in LTC, health literacy, US region, gender, and insurance. Aim 3 followed a mixed-methods convergent design, and data were collected via interviews, focus groups, surveys, recordings, field notes, and web logs. Data collection and analysis were informed by Implementation Mapping and the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Aim 3 activities included a process evaluation that explored intervention fidelity, reach, dose, reactions to the interventions, and, lastly, an exploration of the future sustainability of the interventions and other methods to support vaccine confidence and uptake, with several stakeholder groups. Results: The total analyzable sample for primary outcome assessment was 1387 participants. Engagement rates varied across the interventions, with 20% (n = 85) engaging with the webinar intervention and 77% (n = 364) with the social site. Among the total analyzable sample, the difference in COVID-19 vaccine confidence (primary outcome) between each intervention and usual practice was not statistically significant, evaluated using 1-tailed superiority analyses that failed (webinar vs usual practice group difference (GD), −0.065 [95% CI, −0.122 to −0.009]; social site vs usual practice GD, −0.060 [95% CI, −0.115 to −0.005]). The difference between the 2 interventions was also not statistically significant (GD, −0.005 [95% CI, −0.060 to −0.049]). When only analyzing those who engaged with the interventions, results for secondary outcomes trended in favor of the webinar as compared to the social site and usual practice. Mediation analyses revealed that identification of vaccine information and misinformation was the only variable assessed to have a meaningful mediation effect between the interventions and vaccine confidence. The analysis of heterogeneity of treatment effects revealed no meaningful differences in the interventions’ impact across all participant demographic and belief variables assessed. For aim 3, both interventions were carried out by facilitators with a relatively high degree of adherence to the training and instructions, with a combined average across fidelity domains of 88% for the social site and 75% for the webinar. There were missed opportunities to encourage higher levels of participant engagement in both. Findings from interviews with trial participants and intervention facilitators complemented RCT results by highlighting more positive reactions to the webinar than the social site, including accounts that it provided a welcoming environment for LTCWs to share experiences and concerns. While the social site had features that some participants found engaging, for most, it was not substantively different from other information and social media outlets and even less interesting, given its narrow focus, minimal user activity, and less frequently refreshed content. Survey responses exploring reactions to the interventions also tended to favor the webinar over the other trial arms. In the sustainability phase, we explored adaptations to the webinar that could enhance its impact as well as other approaches to increasing COVID-19 vaccine confidence. Our findings did not support continuing an adapted webinar intervention, particularly in the current context, which presents many challenges. Stakeholders highlighted challenges and provided insight into how future efforts could better create a supportive environment for change via (1) trust in the people who provide information about vaccines; (2) recognition of the diversity of the LTCW population and focus on facilitating culturally aligned conversations; and (3) a workplace culture that explicitly values the health and safety of LTCWs and residents, reinforcing the idea that vaccination should become a core component of that culture. Conclusions: We did not find evidence to support the continued use of either the webinars or social site. However, our study revealed the future efforts that are required to address inadequacies in the LTC workplace, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic, and need attention before efforts to improve attitudes about vaccination are likely to succeed. Limitations: A major limitation was the less-than-anticipated engagement with the webinars, which limited our ability to carry out the intervention as planned, as well as to determine its effectiveness. Also, given the time that had elapsed between intervention exposure and participant interviews exploring reactions to the interventions, there was a degree of poor recall that impacted the depth of feedback provided.

title: Bayesian parameter estimation of SIR and SIRD models for COVID-19 in Indonesia using Metropolis–Hastings and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
abstract: Accurate parameter estimation is essential for reliable epidemic modeling and forecasting.This study presents a Bayesian framework for estimating parameters of the SIR and SIRD epidemiological models using two Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods: Metropolis-Hastings (MH) and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC).Daily COVID-19 surveillance data from Indonesia spanning January to April 2022 are used to estimate the transmission rate (β ), recovery rate (γ), and death rate (κ).Model performance is evaluated through convergence diagnostics (Gelman-Rubin statistic), sampling efficiency (effective sample size, ESS), and predictive accuracy (root mean squared error, RMSE).Results show that the MH algorithm exhibits severe convergence failure, with Gelman-Rubin statistics reaching up to 66.63 and ESS values as low as 7.75, indicating highly autocorrelated and inefficient sampling.In contrast, HMC achieves perfect convergence ( R = 1) across all parameters with ESS values ranging from about 790 to more than 1, 600, reflecting substantially more efficient posterior exploration.Although both algorithms yield high RMSE under the beta prior for β , adopting a lognormal prior reduces the RMSE dramatically-from over one million to approximately 67, 000 for both the SIR and SIRD models when combined with HMC.Among all configurations tested, the SIRD model estimated via HMC with a lognormal prior for β achieves the lowest RMSE (67, 255.57), demonstrating superior predictive performance.These findings suggest that the choice of both the sampling algorithm and the prior distribution critically determines estimation quality
journal: Communications in Mathematical Biology and Neuroscience

title: Resource Loss, Loneliness, and Depressive Symptoms Among Middle-Aged and Older Adults During COVID-19: A Moderated Mediation Analysis and LLM-Based Computational Replication
abstract: Public health emergencies impose lasting mental health burdens worldwide. Conservation of resources (COR) theory suggests resource loss increases depressive symptoms, yet how multiple resources relate to depressive symptoms remains unclear. Using 8485 respondents from the 2020 China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), we estimated a COR-guided moderated mediation model with robust OLS and bootstrap resampling. The 2018 data supplied baseline symptom information for agent initialization. Loneliness was examined as an indicator of relational deprivation and a statistical mediator. We also evaluated 300 DeepSeek-R1 virtual agents calibrated to the real data distribution to test whether large language model (LLM) agents could reproduce these associations. Higher work-time-change scores were associated with more depressive symptoms (B = 0.415, p < 0.001), whereas greater ease in making ends meet (B = −1.216, p < 0.001) was associated with fewer depressive symptoms. Loneliness was positively associated with depressive symptoms (B = 2.913, p < 0.001). Its interaction with intergenerational satisfaction was negative (B = −0.175, p = 0.015), and bootstrap intervals supported indirect associations that varied with relationship satisfaction. The agents reproduced several broad directions of association, but their score distribution and coefficient magnitudes differed from the survey data. These findings support a COR-guided statistical account of resource conditions during COVID-19 and identify the current limits of LLM-based computational replication.

title: Digital mental health interventions for university students during the COVID-19 pandemic and post-pandemic periods: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract: University students experience elevated levels of anxiety, depression, and stress, prompting growing interest in accessible digital psychological interventions. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the effectiveness of digital psychological interventions for university students during the later stages of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and the post-pandemic periods. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), and Cochrane were searched for randomized controlled trials involving university students published between 2020 and June 2026. Random-effects models (Hedges’ g, modified Knapp-Hartung [mKH]) were applied, and Risk of Bias was assessed with Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2). A total of 34 trials (6,544 students, 15 countries) were included. Benefits were significant for depression at 8 weeks (g = 0.48), anxiety at 2 and 8 weeks (g = 0.24 and g = 0.57), stress at 4 weeks (g = 0.23), and post-intervention anxiety (g = 0.75; I 2 = 88.6%), but not for pooled anxiety. Overall, 52.9% of studies were at high Risk of Bias, and only one of six active-comparator trials compared digital with face-to-face delivery. Digital interventions yield modest short-term benefits, but heterogeneity, high Risk of Bias, and a scarcity of face-to-face comparisons limit confidence. http://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/E2C78 , identifier (E2C78).

title: Exposure to cigarettes and e-cigarettes: changes in the expression of inflammatory and SARS-CoV-2 viral entry genes
abstract: Introduction As of 2026, 11% of the UK adult population smoke tobacco cigarettes and 10% vape e-cigarettes. For pandemic preparedness, it is essential to identify populations that may be at a higher risk of infection to ensure more targeted public health advice. Any association between smoking and SARS-CoV-2 infection remains conflicted and there is limited research on the impact of vaping. Methods A human bronchial epithelial cell line cultured at the air-liquid interface was exposed, via suspension, to e-liquid, e-cigarette condensate or tobacco cigarette condensate to determine any direct impacts on respiratory toxicity or genes relating to viral entry and/or inflammation. Results Results demonstrate that e-cigarette condensate had minimal toxicity compared to tobacco cigarette condensate. Additionally, gene expression changes in-vitro suggest exposure to tobacco cigarette condensate increases infection risk compared to e-cigarette condensate exposure. Conclusion Preliminary investigations with SARS-CoV-2 infection reiterates the differing effects of e-cigarette and tobacco cigarette condensate exposure, highlighting the importance of further investigations in both areas to inform public health advice.

source_records.title: Exposure to cigarettes and e-cigarettes: changes in the expression of inflammatory and SARS-CoV-2 viral entry genes
source_records.abstract: Introduction As of 2026, 11% of the UK adult population smoke tobacco cigarettes and 10% vape e-cigarettes. For pandemic preparedness, it is essential to identify populations that may be at a higher risk of infection to ensure more targeted public health advice. Any association between smoking and SARS-CoV-2 infection remains conflicted and there is limited research on the impact of vaping. Results Results demonstrate that e-cigarette condensate had minimal toxicity compared to tobacco cigarette condensate. Conclusion Preliminary investigations with SARS-CoV-2 infection reiterates the differing effects of e-cigarette and tobacco cigarette condensate exposure, highlighting the importance of further investigations in both areas to inform public health advice.

title: Linking personality to COVID-19 attitudes, concerns and biosafety behaviors: meta-analytic foundations for future pandemic preparedness
abstract: Knowledge of behavioral reactions to the COVID-19 pandemic can help manage future reactions and biosafety behaviors, potentially altering the course of future epidemics and pandemics. Personality traits play a role in creating safe environments. We examined the Big Five and Dark Triad personality trait families' associations with biosafety behaviors during the COVID-19 pandemic, a period characterized by strong situational pressures. We also examined personality's associations with COVID-19 concerns and attitudes. Associations with biosafety behaviors, including hygiene, social distancing, self-quarantining, avoiding exposures, and preparatory behaviors, were examined in 92 independent samples comprising 973 effect sizes from over 50 countries. Different traits served different functions: conscientiousness and agreeableness predicted prosocial protective behaviors such as social distancing and hygiene, neuroticism was strongly associated with pandemic-related concerns but not behaviors, and extraversion and openness were linked to adaptation to new safety protocols. Dark Triad traits showed negative associations with collective biosafety behaviors but positive associations with preparatory behaviors, a finding consistent with pandemic responses motivated by self-interest rather than collective welfare. Despite strong situational constraints, personality maintained meaningful associations with behavior. Meta-analytic evidence indicates COVID-19 attitudes, concerns, and biosafety behaviors are in part predicted by personality traits, with implications for public health messaging and understanding individual differences in biosafety-critical occupations.

title: Strategi Kampanye Komunikasi Publik Satgas Covid-19 Nasional dalam Penanganan Covid-19
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic in Indonesia generated significant impacts on public health and the national economy, reflected in rising confirmed cases, economic contraction, and increasing unemployment resulting from physical distancing policies. These conditions required society to adapt to new behavioral norms through structured and effective public communication. This study aims to analyze the public communication campaign strategy implemented by the National COVID-19 Task Force in managing the pandemic and to identify the supporting and inhibiting factors influencing its implementation. The research employed a qualitative approach within a constructivist paradigm using a case study design. Data were collected through in-depth interviews with the public communication division and community members and were analyzed interpretatively. The findings indicate that the campaign strategy was systematically designed with informative and persuasive objectives to enhance public awareness and encourage behavioral change. Messages were science-based and delivered by credible communicators with authentic voices. Furthermore, stakeholder mapping was conducted to strengthen collaborative support, contributing to the development of active and sustainable public participation in pandemic management.

title: Impact of Plasmodium falciparum exposure on SARS-CoV-2 antibody responses, infection and outcomes: a cross-sectional study in Manhiça, Mozambique
abstract: Abstract Background SARS-CoV-2 and Plasmodium falciparum coexist in Africa, raising questions about potential immunological interactions between both pathogens, which could have impacted the COVID-19 pandemic in the continent. However, few studies have assessed the relationship between malaria exposure and SARS-CoV-2 infection, symptomatology, and potential antibody cross-reactivity. Methods We conducted a sero-epidemiological study using plasma samples collected in Mozambique and Spain between 2001 and 2022. IgG, IgM, and IgA responses to spike (S) and nucleocapsid (N) SARS-CoV-2 and blood stage P. falciparum antigens were measured using a multiplex assay to evaluate potential cross-reactivity between antibodies. COVID-19 pre-pandemic samples from Mozambique ( n = 175) and Spain ( n = 35) were used to assess baseline IgG cross-reactivity. Post-pandemic samples from 2,576 individuals in Manhiça, Mozambique (2021–2022), were analyzed to examine associations between malaria exposure, quantified by a composite malaria IgG score, and SARS-CoV-2 infection, seropositivity and COVID-19 symptomatology. Statistical tests included t-tests, Spearman correlations, and unadjusted logistic regressions. Results The quantitative suspension array antibody assay to assess SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity achieved high sensitivity (IgG: 85%; IgA: 75%) and specificity (> 93%), with best performance for S and receptor-binding domain (RBD) antigens. Pre-pandemic African samples showed significantly higher anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgG reactivity than the European ones ( p < 0.0001). In pre-pandemic samples, moderate correlations were observed between anti– P. falciparum and anti–SARS-CoV-2 IgG (e.g., RBD vs. EBA-175, r = 0.41, p < 0.001). In post-pandemic samples, correlations weakened with rising SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence. Prior exposure to malaria was not associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection, SARS-CoV-2 seropositivity or COVID-19 symptomatology. Conclusions Our findings demonstrate evidence of serological cross-reactivity between antibodies against P. falciparum and SARS-CoV-2 in pre-pandemic African samples. These results highlight the importance of sero-surveillance approaches that account for co-endemic pathogens to better inform public health strategies in these co-endemic regions. Clinical Trial Not applicable.

title: Social and Occupational Experiences and Mental Health Effects of Quarantine Among Physicians in India During COVID-19: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background and Aims: Medical professionals faced social, occupational, and financial challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic. This study described these experiences and the perceived effect of quarantine on mental health among physicians in India. Materials and Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional online survey included 558 registered medical practitioners recruited purposively between February and August 2022. A study-specific questionnaire assessed social, occupational and financial experiences and asked, “Did the quarantine period affect your mental health status?” This binary item did not establish the direction or severity of the effect. Results: Overall, 210 of 558 respondents (37.6%) answered yes to the question about a mental health effect of quarantine. The question did not establish whether the effect was adverse or its severity. A drastic reduction in income was reported by 267 participants (47.8%), no change in financial health by 231 (41.4%), and cessation of practice by 60 (10.8%). New insurance purchase for the respondent or a family member was reported by 174 of 558 respondents (31.2%); this is not a percentage of the 162 respondents without personal insurance before the pandemic. Conclusions: The reported social, occupational, and financial experiences support consideration of confidential staff support, safe reporting of public incidents and assistance with work disruption. These are practical priorities for further evaluation, not interventions tested by this survey. The mental health item does not establish deterioration or clinical need.

title: Evaluating the Life rooms social model of health for those impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: In late 2021, The Life Rooms was commissioned by Public Health Liverpool to deliver a community-based mental health prevention offer to support individuals and communities post COVID-19 pandemic. For a 12-month period, The Life Rooms’ services, including learning and social prescribing were delivered across a number of community sites in Liverpool including libraries, one stop shops and children’s centres. The evaluation sought to explore the impact of providing The Life Rooms service peripatetically in a series of strategically located community sites with a view to providing more effective services for the community and to develop The Life Rooms’ Social Model of Health. The evaluation employed a mixed methods approach comprising qualitative and quantitative data collected through service user surveys, case studies, interviews, a focus group, and the Recovering Quality of Life (ReQoL-10) outcome measure. Audit data in the form of activity data and demographics were also collected and analysed. The ReQoL-10 outcome measure was completed by 50 service users, before and after accessing support from The Life Rooms. The questionnaire was completed by 75 service users, and 19 service users provided a case study. Three service users participated in a focus group and two service users participated in one-to-one semi-structured interviews. During the project 1,162 individuals registered with The Life Rooms via the Public Health sites. While the overall change in ReQoL-10 scores was not statistically significant, a significant improvement was observed among service users who accessed both elements of The Life Rooms offer—the Pathways Advice Service and the psychoeducational learning courses. Quantitative and qualitative findings indicated that many individuals experienced a broad range of benefits. Expanding the geographical footprint of The Life Rooms’ services and working peripatetically has allowed The Life Rooms and Public Health Liverpool to work with people across places, better tailoring services to meet their needs and preferences so that they are designed and delivered more effectively.

title: COVID-19 impact on households’ energy poverty and clean energy transition in China
abstract: Abstract The COVID-19 pandemic has had a profound yet understudied impact on energy poverty and clean energy transition among households. Using at least 6000 and up to 12,000 household longitudinal data from the China Family Panel Studies from 2014 through 2022, this study implements multiple empirical strategies to assess these effects on urban and rural Chinese households. Our findings reveal that the pandemic disrupted the pre-existing trend of rising electricity usage and exacerbated energy inequality, as indicated by shifts in the Lorenz curves of household energy expenditure. In particular, the energy poverty of rural households increased more rapidly than that of their urban counterparts in the post-pandemic era. Moreover, the growth rates of energy poverty incidence, depth, and intensity decelerated following the outbreak, suggesting a partial regression of energy poverty alleviation interventions, particularly in western and certain central regions compared to the more developed eastern Chinese provinces. Finally, the pandemic shock further intensified household energy poverty, whereby structurally advantaged households demonstrated resilience, but marginalized households experienced deepened deprivation. These insights highlight the urgency of implementing affordable, equitable, and resilience-based clean energy policy interventions in and beyond China.
