title: Pharmacovigilance of Maternal Vaccines in Africa: An Analysis of Reporting Patterns from VigiBase ® , 2010-2024.
abstract: BACKGROUND Maternal immunisation is an effective strategy for reducing morbidity and mortality in pregnant women and neonates, yet it requires close safety monitoring, but safety surveillance capacity in Africa has historically been limited. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic provided an unprecedented opportunity to evaluate Africa's capacity for maternal vaccine pharmacovigilance and assess whether pandemic-era gains could be sustained. OBJECTIVE To characterize maternal vaccine safety reporting from Africa in VigiBase® (2010-2024), compare reporting patterns for COVID-19 and non-COVID vaccines, and identify priorities for strengthening maternal immunization safety surveillance METHODS: A retrospective descriptive analysis of individual case safety reports submitted by African countries to VigiBase®, the World Health Organization global pharmacovigilance database, was conducted for January 2010 to December 2024. Reports were identified using the Uppsala Monitoring Centre pregnancy algorithm and classified according to the Brighton Collaboration Global Alignment of Immunisation Safety Assessment in Pregnancy adverse events following the maternal immunisation framework. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used to compare COVID-19 and non-COVID vaccine reporting patterns, and a Mann-Whitney U test was used to compare pre-pandemic and pandemic annual reporting volumes. RESULTS Africa contributed 817 of 44,316 global maternal vaccine safety reports (1.84%), submitted by 33 of 55 African countries. Of these, 573 (70.1%) were associated with COVID-19 vaccines and 244 (29.9%) with non-COVID-19 vaccines. Annual reporting increased markedly during the pandemic period (median 183.0 vs 4.5 reports/year; Mann-Whitney U test = 0.0, p = 0.004, effect size r = 0.785), with Africa's global share rising from 0.49 to 2.48%. A total of 1619 adverse events were recorded across 817 reports. Adverse events following maternal immunisation category distributions differed significantly between vaccine types (χ2 = 200.6, df = 5, p < 0.001): COVID-19 vaccines were predominantly associated with maternal systemic events (36.9%) and unclassifiable reports (36.1%), whereas non-COVID vaccines generated proportionally more pregnancy outcome-specific events (25.3%) and fetal adverse events (8.1%). Physicians submitted the most reports but had the highest unclassifiable rate (52.3%), significantly exceeding all other reporter groups (χ2 = 125.0, df = 4, p < 0.001). Consumer reporting rose from one pre-pandemic report to 82 reports during 2021-24. CONCLUSIONS The COVID-19 pandemic catalysed a substantial expansion in maternal vaccine pharmacovigilance in Africa, demonstrating the continent's capacity to scale up surveillance rapidly. However, persistent gaps in data completeness and uneven country participation highlight the need for sustained embedded surveillance as new maternal vaccines targeting respiratory syncytial virus and group B Streptococcus are introduced.

title: Pharmacological inhibition of coronavirus replication via modulation of host lipid metabolism
abstract: The emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) in 2019 and the subsequent coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic highlighted the urgent need for novel therapeutic approaches. Coronaviruses rely extensively on host cell metabolic pathways to support their propagation, and efficient viral replication requires the extensive remodelling of host cell membranes. This includes the formation of specialized membranous structures known as replication organelles that accommodate viral RNA synthesis in the cytoplasm of the infected cell. Other processes depending on host membranes are viral entry, the acquisition of the coronavirus envelope from intracellular membrane compartments and the post-translational conjugation of lipids to certain viral proteins. The endogenous pathways involved in these pivotal steps of coronavirus replication represent attractive targets for host-directed antiviral therapy, which may also reduce the emergence of resistance that often limits the efficacy of direct-acting antiviral drug treatment. Accordingly, recent studies have identified a range of small-molecule inhibitors that target lipid metabolism pathways and display promising antiviral activity against coronaviruses. In this review, we examine the pharmacological modulation of lipid metabolism with small-molecule inhibitors as an antiviral strategy against SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses and discuss the strengths, limitations and translational challenges associated with these compounds. We further consider how advances in our understanding of such virus-host metabolic interactions may facilitate the development of broadly active host-directed antivirals, contributing to pandemic preparedness against known and newly emerging coronaviruses.

This includes the formation of specialized membranous structures known as replication organelles that accommodate viral RNA synthesis in the cytoplasm of the infected cell. Other processes depending on host membranes are viral entry, the acquisition of the coronavirus envelope from intracellular membrane compartments and the post-translational conjugation of lipids to certain viral proteins. The endogenous pathways involved in these pivotal steps of coronavirus replication represent attractive targets for host-directed antiviral therapy, which may also reduce the emergence of resistance that often limits the efficacy of direct-acting antiviral drug treatment. Accordingly, recent studies have identified a range of small-molecule inhibitors that target lipid metabolism pathways and display promising antiviral activity against coronaviruses. In this review, we examine the pharmacological modulation of lipid metabolism with small-molecule inhibitors as an antiviral strategy against SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses and discuss the strengths, limitations and translational challenges associated with these compounds. We further consider how advances in our understanding of such virus-host metabolic interactions may facilitate the development of broadly active host-directed antivirals, contributing to pandemic preparedness against known and newly emerging coronaviruses.

title: Repeated exposure to a conserved antigen drives dynamic clonal and epitope succession
abstract: Defining the dynamics of T cell memory formation with epitope-level resolution can inform vaccine design. Longitudinal T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing after COVID-19 mRNA vaccination has enabled detailed tracking of T cell responses; however, connecting expanded clonotypes following antigen exposure to their cognate epitopes remains a challenge due to limited curated paired /{beta}TCR information. To fill this gap, we used TIRTL-seq to identify paired /{beta}TCRs from CD8+ T cell lineages associated with mRNA immunization in serial samples across 38 healthy donors over multiple rounds of vaccinations. Vaccine-associated paired /{beta}TCRs, identified based on their longitudinal kinetics, were grouped according to sequence similarity to infer their shared epitope specificities. We assigned epitope specificity to 1,109 clonotypes, recognizing 15 SARS-CoV-2 spike targets, identifying multiple previously undescribed responses, and confirming putative specificities experimentally. This approach uncovered a striking pattern of clonal succession in anti-spike T cell memory lineages resulting from repeated vaccination, characterized by a transition from low-avidity clones recognizing conserved coronavirus epitopes to high-avidity clones targeting epitopes unique to SARS-CoV-2. These results highlight the surprisingly dynamic responses underlying homologous boosting, suggest avenues for improving vaccine strategies, and pave the way for repertoire-based monitoring of antigen-specific T cell immunity.

title: Trends of delayed healthcare access in ocular injuries: a multicenter study in community hospitals, Central Thailand.
abstract: Aim To determine the annual trends and risk factors for delayed access to care in community hospitals across Central Thailand-an area with high occupational injury risk. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study analyzed data from four community hospitals in Central Thailand over six years (October 1, 2018-September 17, 2024). Patients aged ≥20y with ocular injuries, identified via International Classification of Diseases-10 (ICD-10) codes, were included. Demographics, injury characteristics, and care-seeking behaviors were recorded. Delayed access was defined as presentation >24h post-injury. Linear and logistic regression models were used to identify associated risk factors. Annual fiscal trends were analyzed to assess year-to-year patterns in delayed healthcare access. Results Among 6571 ocular injury cases, 4034 (61.4%) were male, with median age 43y [interquartile range (IQR) 31-57y], and 3983 (79.3%) were manual laborers. Delayed healthcare access was observed in 2426 cases (36.9%). Significant risk factors included age ≥60y [aOR: 1.55; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.32-1.82], visits to F2-level hospitals [adjusted odds ratio (aOR): 2.03; 95%CI: 1.73-2.38], and outpatient visits (aOR: 14.01; 95%CI: 12.18-16.12). In F2 hospitals, subgroup analysis revealed a U-shaped reduction in delayed healthcare access for ocular injuries during the COVID-19 pandemic (2019-2021), adjusted for age and gender. Conclusion This first in-depth study of ocular injuries in Central Thailand's community hospitals found persistently high delayed presentations, with older age, F2 hospital visits, and outpatient department (OPD) attendance as key contributing factors. The trend during the COVID-19 pandemic highlights the important role of lower-tier community hospitals in providing prompt and accessible care for patients. Strengthening healthcare infrastructure and public awareness is essential to ensure timely care and reduce preventable vision-related complications.

title: Comparison of Dissemination of Aerosol and Splatter during Ultrasonic Scaling using Different Masks: A Pilot Study with Relevance to Respiratory Infection Transmission
abstract: Abstract Background: Dentists are routinely exposed to a high amount of micro-organism load due to primarily being responsible for the treatment of the structures if the mouth – which is a well-known source of huge bacterial loads. Also, as COVID-19 recently affected the entire world, masks thus were considered to act as a comprehensive strategy of measures to suppress transmission. However, the relevance of aerosol and respiratory infection control extends beyond COVID-19, as respiratory pathogens including seasonal influenza viruses such as influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, commonly referred to as swine flu, influenza A(H3N2), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and other respiratory viruses continue to circulate and may be transmitted through respiratory particles. Aim: To compare the dissemination of aerosol and splatter during ultrasonic scaling using different masks. Method: In this study we evaluated the dissemination of four masks that is N-95 with respirator, N-95 without respirator, a combination of cloth mask and N-95 without respirator, and normal surgical mask by calculating the surface are of filter paper with the help of a previously marked scale which was divided into one-centimeter squares. Results: Best protection was seen to be offered by the combined use of the double masking – N-95 without filter plus cloth mask, followed by N-95 mask alone and then the surgical mask.

title: Respiratory Infections at Mass Gatherings: A Travel-Medicine Review with Hajj and Umrah as a Longitudinal Case Study.
abstract: Background Mass gatherings combine international mobility with dense, repeated contact and can amplify respiratory infections across travel corridors. Hajj, Umrah and Kumbh Mela, offer a uniquely recurrent case study, while other religious or sporting mega-events, and music or cultural festivals provide contrasting exposure systems. Methods A focused narrative review was conducted of peer-reviewed studies, systematic and scoping reviews, and authoritative public-health guidance. Searches and project evidence synthesis prioritized publications from January 2021 to August 2026, with selected foundational sources. We examined respiratory symptoms, laboratory detections, clinical disease, vaccination, antimicrobial use and resistance, surveillance, environmental modifiers, and pre-, during-, and post-travel practice. No meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias scoring was undertaken. Results Respiratory risk is determined less by attendance alone than by contact intensity, duration, ventilation, vocalization, shared accommodation, traveler susceptibility, and pathogen circulation. Recent Hajj evidence confirms a substantial burden of respiratory symptoms and clinical consultations, but estimates vary because denominators range from volunteers and tested samples to healthcare encounters. Rhinovirus, influenza, SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and bacterial pneumonia remain important. There is continued abuse of antibiotics for predominantly viral syndromes and acquisition of resistant organisms link individual care to global antimicrobial resistance. Syndromic, laboratory, event-based, genomic, and wastewater surveillance are complementary, not interchangeable. Heat, dust, air quality, fatigue, and differential access to protective infrastructure modify respiratory symptoms, severity, and care seeking. Comparative events share mechanisms but not directly transferable rates. Conclusions Travel-medicine practice should treat mass gatherings as longitudinal exposure systems spanning preparation, transport, the event, and return. Layered vaccination, risk-based masking, ventilation and crowd-flow measures, prompt diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship, and explicit travel histories, can reduce respiratory morbidity while preserving denominator discipline and access to protective infrastructure.

title: Global research trends on healthcare-associated infections in the context of natural disasters, epidemics and pandemics.
abstract: IntroductionHealthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a serious public health concern. HAIs risk increases extraordinary events such as natural disasters, epidemics, and pandemics.Material and MethodsThis study analyzes publication trends related to HAIs in these contexts using bibliometric methods. Publications on HAIs related to natural disasters, epidemics, and pandemics from Scopus without year or document type restrictions were analyzed using VOSviewer to assess trends, keyword co-occurrence, citations, and country productivity.ResultsA total of 774 publications were analyzed, including 749 on epidemics/pandemics, and 25 on natural disasters. Publications increased notably during epidemics/pandemics, especially during COVID-19. The USA and China were leading publishing countries. Keyword analysis showed that "covıd-19" and "SARS-CoV-2" were most frequent in epidemic-/pandemic-related research, while "earthquake" appeared commonly in disaster-related studies.Before 2015, "nosocomial infections" was widely used, later replaced by "healthcare-associated infections." From 2018, studies focused more on multidrug-resistant organisms like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae . Recent years emphasized ventilator-associated pneumonia, mechanical ventilation, and Clostridioides difficile infections. Limited keyword data prevented overlay visualization for natural disasters.ConclusionsResearch on HAIs intensifies during epidemiological crises but remains limited for natural disasters, highlighting the need for further interdisciplinary studies to better understand and reduce HAI risks.

HAIs risk increases extraordinary events such as natural disasters, epidemics, and pandemics.Material and MethodsThis study analyzes publication trends related to HAIs in these contexts using bibliometric methods. Publications on HAIs related to natural disasters, epidemics, and pandemics from Scopus without year or document type restrictions were analyzed using VOSviewer to assess trends, keyword co-occurrence, citations, and country productivity.ResultsA total of 774 publications were analyzed, including 749 on epidemics/pandemics, and 25 on natural disasters. Publications increased notably during epidemics/pandemics, especially during COVID-19. The USA and China were leading publishing countries. Keyword analysis showed that "covıd-19" and "SARS-CoV-2" were most frequent in epidemic-/pandemic-related research, while "earthquake" appeared commonly in disaster-related studies.Before 2015, "nosocomial infections" was widely used, later replaced by "healthcare-associated infections." From 2018, studies focused more on multidrug-resistant organisms like methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae . Recent years emphasized ventilator-associated pneumonia, mechanical ventilation, and Clostridioides difficile infections. Limited keyword data prevented overlay visualization for natural disasters.ConclusionsResearch on HAIs intensifies during epidemiological crises but remains limited for natural disasters, highlighting the need for further interdisciplinary studies to better understand and reduce HAI risks.

title: Escala de niveles de intensidad terapéutica. Desarrollo y utilidad para la toma de decisiones clínicas en un hospital universitario
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop and implement a therapeutic intensity level (NIT-Mar) scale in a hospital consortium and evaluate its use. METHODS: Adaptation of a therapeutic intensity scale through an expert panel and subsequent evaluation based on a retrospective observational study in patients who died from SARS-CoV-2 infection between March and June 2020 in a university hospital consortium. The following were analyzed: clinical characteristics, use and change of the scale, consensus in decision-making, and concordance between the assigned therapeutic intensity level and the therapeutic measures applied. RESULTS: A total of 210 patients were included, with 74.8% assigned a NIT. No significant differences were found in age, gender, or comorbidities between patients with and without NIT. Decision-making consensus was achieved in 87.9% of cases, mainly among professionals (77%) and families (72.6%), but only in 12.7% with the patient. In 49.7% of cases, the NIT was modified during hospitalization. Concordance between the assigned NIT and applied treatments was 85.3%. CONCLUSION: The NIT-Mar scale was widely used from its implementation, facilitating decision-making in high-demand healthcare settings. Its flexibility allowed adjustments in therapeutic intensity according to patient evolution. This tool can improve communication between teams, care planning and patient safety.

title: Class-switched CD21 + CD27 + memory B cells as a predictive immunological marker of vaccine-induced humoral responsiveness in Common Variable Immunodeficiency
abstract: Abstract Common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) is a clinically heterogeneous primary immunodeficiency characterized by defective humoral immunity and highly variable vaccine-induced antibody responses. However, in-depth characterization of vaccine-specific B cell responses in CVID remains limited, hindering our understanding of the cellular basis of this heterogeneity. Here, we investigated how CVID affects formation and maintenance of antigen-specific B cell responses following COVID-19 mRNA-based vaccination of patients who either do (responders; R) or do not (non-responders; NR) seroconvert. The evolution of the spike (S)-specific B cell compartment was longitudinally investigated after vaccination and compared to RSV-F-specific B cells, as a historically encountered antigen, and the total B cell compartment. CVID-NR patients showed pronouncedly reduced S-specific B cell numbers at all time points compared to CVID-R and healthy donors. Additionally, the S-specific B cell compartment showed a predominantly naïve, unswitched phenotype. CVID-R exhibited a delayed S-specific B cell differentiation, with a markedly naïve, unswitched response after the first vaccination, an enhanced response after the second vaccination with reduced IgG+ memory B cells, and a fully established S-specific B cell compartment 6 months after vaccination. Analysis of the general B cell compartment showed strongly diminished class-switched B cell populations in NR patients, emerging as a predictive immunological marker for vaccine-induced humoral responsiveness in CVID. Together, these findings reveal distinct cellular alterations underlying vaccine responsiveness in patients with CVID and identify potential correlates of humoral vaccine responses, stablishing a framework for more personalized immune monitoring strategies in CVID.

title: Ultrafast alignment-free detection of viral genome variation with bronko
abstract: As viral sequencing datasets continue to grow, traditional alignment-based variant calling pipelines are becoming computationally prohibitive. To address these challenges, we developed bronko, an ultrafast alignment-free framework for detecting viral variation directly from sequencing data. The novel computational approach implemented in bronko allows scaling to massive viral sequencing datasets and has four key components: i) a locality-sensitive bucketing function to rapidly identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) relative to reference(s), ii) a direct k -mer count pseudo-mapping approach that approximates a pileup without alignment, iii) a greedy de novo assembly algorithm to reconstruct mutation-dense regions and indels and iv) a streaming-based sliding window outlier test to estimate baseline noise across the genome and precisely differentiate real minor variants from noise. Together, these components yield near-linear computational complexity with respect to sequencing depth, enabling bronko to process thousands of viral samples rapidly on modest hardware. Our results are threefold: 1) On simulated amplicon sequencing, bronko recovers variants with higher precision and comparable recall to existing tools while running up to one to three orders of magnitude faster; 2) bronko generates sequence alignments directly from sequencing data, with SNP content nearly identical to that of whole-genome alignment while also running in a fraction of the time, and 3) applying bronko to longitudinal sequencing data from chronically infected SARS-CoV-2 patients revealed consistent patterns of intrahost diversification and adaptive mutations over time. Altogether, these results demonstrate bronko's potential as a scalable tool for large-scale viral genomic analyses, overcoming longstanding computational barriers for intrahost and interhost characterization of viral variation.

title: [THE STRUCTURAL AND DYNAMIC CHARACTERISTICS OF THE DISEASES OF BLOOD CIRCULATION ORGANS IN THE KYRGYZ REPUBLIC].
abstract: The diseases of circulatory system continue to occupy leading positions in structure of morbidity and mortality of population, remaining one of key public health problems. The purpose of the study is to investigate dynamics of primary morbidity and prevalence of diseases of circulatory system by main nosological forms among adult and adolescent population of the Kyrgyz Republic in 2018-2024. The study used official data from the Center for E-Health Care that was analyzed using retrospective, statistical and comparative analytical methods. It was found that indicators of primary morbidity and prevalence were characterized by pronounced variability with greatest increase in 2022, against the background of decrease in 2020-2021, that may be due to changes in availability of medical care in period of COVID-19 pandemic. The highest levels of morbidity and prevalence were found for hypertension, coronary heart disease and cerebrovascular diseases. Some nosologies, including myocardial infarction and other peripheral vascular diseases, demonstrated sharp increase in indicators, suggesting changes in disease detection and health care seeking behavior of population. The obtained results confirm necessity to improve system of monitoring, prevention and early detection of cardiovascular diseases, especially among high-risk groups.

title: The Contribution of a Health Society to Immunization in Saudi Arabia: a Community Case study of the Waey Association for Community Health
abstract: Background: Non-Profit Organizations (NPOs) are long-standing partners in immunization, yet documented examples from state-led health systems remain scarce. This case study examines how a Saudi health society contributes to immunization through a surge workforce and vaccine demand beyond childhood. Methods: A community case study was conducted through document analysis of the program documentation of the Waey Association for Community Health, compiled for the 8th Saudi International Vaccination Forum (Riyadh, 2026). Activity domains were profiled against an explicit inclusion rule, reported outputs were converted into derived indicators, and each domain was coded against seven NPO roles drawn from a global scoping review; the findings were then synthesized into an explanatory model. Results: Six immunization domains addressing coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), human papillomavirus (HPV), seasonal influenza, and adult vaccination were identified, alongside two supporting activities. Deployment to COVID-19 vaccination centers mobilized 313 volunteers for 24,778 hours (79.2 hours per volunteer); the 2024 to 2025 community vaccination program mobilized 336 volunteers for 9,628 hours and reached 14,281 beneficiaries through 17 activities. The COVID-19 deployment thus supplied 72.0% of combined hours from 48.2% of volunteers. Four of seven NPO roles were represented, led by service delivery and demand generation. Conclusions: The society functioned as a reservoir of trained surge capacity and as a channel for vaccine demand among adolescents and adults. Both functions drew on shared assets, and a minimum reporting standard covering doses, unique beneficiaries, volunteer hours, and population denominators would allow them to be evaluated.

title: Model-Informed Evaluation of Drug-Drug Interaction Recommendations for Amlodipine and Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir: A Hypothesis-Generating Analysis.
abstract: While nirmatrelvir-ritonavir effectively prevents severe COVID-19, its ritonavir component causes significant drug-drug interactions (DDIs). Current guidelines suggest mitigating this interaction by halving the amlodipine dose or moving to every-other-day (EOD) dosing, then resuming the standard regimen 3-5 days post-antiviral treatment. We applied physiologically based pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PBPK-PD) modeling to evaluate the effects of these recommendations on systolic blood pressure (SBP) control. SARS-CoV-2 inpatients who received nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (October-December 2022) and were exposed to potential DDIs were identified. An amlodipine PBPK-PD model incorporating the diurnal variation of SBP was developed. The model was validated using amlodipine PK studies, including in DDI scenarios, while the PD model was validated against SBP data collected during amlodipine treatment. Simulations were performed in representative virtual populations, comprising various amlodipine doses and regimens, during and after nirmatrelvir-ritonavir therapy. 362/1729 (20.9%) drugs from 166/217 (76.5%) patients were identified to have potential DDIs implicating nirmatrelvir-ritonavir. Amlodipine was a common interacting drug (64/362, 17.7%) and often prescribed without dose adjustment (63%). Our simulations supported that continuing amlodipine during therapy may lead to SBP ≤100 mmHg at daily doses of ≥5 mg, while discontinuation may lead to SBP >130-150 mmHg. Halving the amlodipine dose during nirmatrelvir-ritonavir treatment could provide more stable SBP control than EOD dosing. Resuming usual doses 3 days after nirmatrelvir-ritonavir could be more important in those receiving 7.5 and 10 mg of amlodipine. DDIs between nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and amlodipine were common. Our simulations evaluated current dose adjustment recommendations for amlodipine with mechanistic quantitative reasoning.

Our simulations evaluated current dose adjustment recommendations for amlodipine with mechanistic quantitative reasoning.

title: Single-Component Photo-Crosslinked Lipoic Acid Functionalized Mucin Hydrogels: Dynamic Mucus Mimetics for Antiviral Protection
abstract: Native mucus protects epithelial surfaces through viscoelastic networks of disulfide-linked mucins. However, commercially available mucins often fail to reconstitute comparable mechanical and barrier properties, while synthetic and hybrid mucus mimetics require polymeric crosslinkers that may alter mucus-like composition. Inspired by the native architecture, we directly functionalized porcine gastric and bovine submaxillary mucins with α-lipoic acid to develop a single-component, photo-crosslinkable hydrogels. Upon UV irradiation (365 nm), the modified mucins rapidly form disulfide-crosslinked networks without added photo-initiator/ polymeric crosslinkers, two orders of magnitude faster as compared with PEG-SH approaches. The resulting mucin-lipoic acid (MUC-LA) hydrogels exhibit mucus-relevant properties, including tunable viscoelasticity, redox responsiveness, self-healing, and size-dependent restrictions on nanoparticle transport. In transwell-based infection models, MUC-LA hydrogels (2-3%) mimicking the healthy airway mucus (G′ ≈ 10-20 Pa) suppress epithelial infection by SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. Crosslinked MUC-LA provides greater protection against SARS-CoV-2 than the non-crosslinked, whereas both formulations suppress influenza A infection, suggesting distinct contributions from network formation and mucin-associated interactions. These findings establish a dynamic, mucus-mimetic platform integrating rapid photo-gelation, controllable mechanics, selective transport, and antiviral barrier functionality. MUC-LA hydrogels offer opportunities to investigate mucosal transport and host-pathogen interactions, with potential applications in drug delivery, and as biomaterials.

title: Travelers and Human–Animal Pathogen Transmission: A One Health Review of Zoonotic and Reverse Zoonotic Diseases
abstract: Background: International travel can accelerate the geographic spread of zoonotic pathogens and, under certain circumstances, contribute to epidemic or pandemic dissemination. Travelers may also transmit human pathogens to wildlife at tourism interfaces, acting as intermediaries in zoonotic and reverse zoonotic transmission. Methods: Archived WHO and ECDC reports were screened for major zoonotic outbreaks in which international travel contributed to cross-border spread. PubMed and Scopus were searched for studies of human-to-wildlife transmission involving tourists, visitors, or travelers and traveler behaviors that could facilitate transmission. Results: Among 14 major zoonotic outbreaks, travelers commonly acted as spreaders following initial animal-to-human spillover by importing infections into new regions, sometimes resulting in onward transmission. This pattern was prominent with respiratory infections such as SARS, MERS, influenza, and COVID-19 and vector-borne infections such as Oropouche and Zika. Twenty-one studies reported possible or confirmed reverse zoonotic transmission at human–wildlife tourism interfaces. Pathogens included respiratory viruses, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, enteric pathogens, and antimicrobial-resistant pathogens. Affected wildlife included great apes, primates, elephants, felines, carnivorans, ungulates, avians, reptiles, and urban-adapted wildlife in national parks, zoological parks, rehabilitation centers, and semi-urban parks. Five additional studies documented risky tourist behaviors, including close approach to, physical contact with, and feeding and visiting wildlife while having respiratory symptoms, and inadequate vaccination against measles, influenza, and polio. Conclusions: Travelers can influence transmission bidirectionally by disseminating zoonotic pathogens and exposing wildlife to human pathogens. Travel medicine should incorporate wildlife-protective counseling on distancing, hygiene, waste disposal, and immunization alongside conventional traveler protection.

title: Readiness Among Female Community Health Volunteers to Deliver Community Based Tobacco Cessation Counseling in Rural Nepal: A Two-phase Mixed-methods Study
abstract: Tobacco cessation support is largely absent from health facilities in Nepal, particularly in rural areas. Female community health volunteers(FCHVs) serve communities across the country and could help extend cessation services, but it was unknown whether they can deliver tobacco cessation counseling. We evaluated their readiness to do so. Guided by the Health Belief Model, we conducted a two-phase mixed-methods evaluation with 28 volunteers in rural mid-Western Nepal. We held eight focus group discussions exploring the volunteers’ knowledge, confidence, and barriers to providing counseling, in two phases, eleven months apart. After the first phase we delivered a tobacco cessation training using lectures and role play, followed by a refresher training after the second phase, and we administered surveys before and after each training. We analyzed the qualitative data with deductive and inductive coding to identify themes, analyzed the surveys with descriptive statistics and Fisher’s exact test, and integrated the two sources to assess convergence and complementarity. The volunteers’ mean age was 48 years, one third had secondary education, and three quarters had served as volunteers for more than ten years. We identified five themes. In the first phase, volunteers had good knowledge of tobacco, its health effects, and cessation measures, recognized a role for themselves in counseling, and asked for regular training. In the second phase, their knowledge and confidence had improved, including trust that quitting is achievable, although some misconceptions and hesitation remained. They described personal, social, and policy-level barriers, such as community hesitation to engage in counseling, limited time, and easy access to tobacco products. Community receptivity to counseling improved over time, but the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted their efforts. Surveys showed that volunteers recognized their role and routinely provided counseling, while knowledge, confidence, and perceived barriers remained relatively stable across surveys; concerns about inadequate incentives and motivation rose from 25% to 57.1% between phases. The qualitative and survey findings converged and complemented each other, with the qualitative data providing depth and the surveys showing numerical trends. Female community health volunteers want to provide tobacco cessation counseling, showed good knowledge and confidence, and reported growing community receptivity, but they face several barriers. Qualitative findings suggest that training improved their knowledge and confidence. Policymakers should consider addressing system-level barriers, including training support and the availability of tobacco products, and integrating volunteers into cessation services. Before wider adoption, future studies should evaluate whether volunteer-led tobacco cessation counseling is clinically effective.

title: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure versus High-Flow Nasal Oxygen in Adults with Pneumonia-Related Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and high-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) are both used to avert invasive mechanical ventilation in patients with pneumonia-related acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF), but head-to-head evidence comparing these two modalities specifically, rather than each against conventional oxygen, remains fragmented. We searched major databases for studies enrolling adults with pneumonia-related AHRF, including COVID-19-related pneumonia, managed with CPAP versus HFNO. The prespecified primary outcome was intubation within 30 days; secondary outcomes were time to intubation, in-hospital, 30-day, and 90-day mortality, and length of hospital stay. Seven studies (n=1,551), met the inclusion criteria. CPAP was associated with a significantly lower risk of intubation within 30 days than HFNO (RR 0.75 [0.65-0.86], p<0.0001; I2=33%; moderate certainty of evidence). This benefit was significant among patients with COVID-19 pneumonia (RR 0.75 [0.65-0.86], p<0.0001) but not among those with non-COVID-19 pneumonia (RR 0.67 [0.31-1.45]), although no significant subgroup interaction was detected (p=0.78). CPAP was also associated with a significantly longer time to intubation than HFNO (MD 22.27 hours [16.22-28.33]). No significant differences were observed between CPAP and HFNO for 30-day mortality, 90-day mortality, in-hospital mortality, or length of hospital stay. The reduction in intubation was attenuated but persisted when the analysis was restricted to the four randomized trials (RR 0.81 [0.70-0.95]; I2=0%). In adults with pneumonia-related AHRF, CPAP probably reduces the risk of intubation compared with HFNO without conferring a mortality advantage or reducing length of stay. HFNO remains a reasonable, generally better-tolerated alternative.

title: C-terminal engineered human H-chain ferritin for peptide loading within the protein nanocage.
abstract: Self-assembling proteins are widely used in bionanotechnology due to their biocompatibility, non-toxicity, structural stability, and easy functionalization. Ferritins (Fts) are particularly attractive systems, as they assemble into highly ordered nanocages with a hollow internal cavity. Their assembly and disassembly can be modulated by various protocols, such as changes in pH or the use of denaturing agents, enabling their application in molecular encapsulation and drug delivery. However, the efficiency of encapsulation remains challenging, often resulting in low or heterogeneous loading and incomplete protein recovery. Here, we load peptides into the core of the human H-chain ferritin (hHFt) by genetically fusing them to the C-terminus of the Ft subunit, a region facing the inner cavity. As model peptides, we used fragments derived from the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein sharing similar physicochemical properties but different charges. The structure of the functionalized nanocages was assessed using techniques like transmission electron microscopy, native gel electrophoresis, and X-ray crystallography. High-resolution structural analysis revealed interesting conformational changes in the hHFt BC-loop associated with C-terminal functionalization, while the overall nanocage architecture is preserved. Additionally, NMR measurements of the transverse relaxation (T 2 ) of a target peptide demonstrated that the nanocages do not expose the fused peptides under native conditions, but upon disassembly, can efficiently expose them, demonstrating that C-terminal genetic functionalization of ferritin nanocages is a robust and effective approach for nanobiotechnological applications.

title: Cross-ancestry proteome-wide mendelian randomization of plasma proteins and breast cancer susceptibility.
abstract: The plasma proteome may help connect inherited breast cancer susceptibility to biologically interpretable and potentially actionable pathways, but proteome-wide evidence across ancestries remains limited. We conducted proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses of breast cancer risk using cis-protein quantitative trait loci for 1,962 distinct plasma proteins from 34,557 European-ancestry participants in the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project. Breast cancer genome-wide association studies included 156,901 cases and 204,634 controls of European, East Asian, and African ancestries. Ancestry-specific MR estimates were combined by fixed-effects meta-analysis. Candidate proteins were further evaluated through subtype-specific and reverse-direction MR analyses, statistical colocalization, replication in independent European and East Asian proteomic datasets, and analyses of associations between protein polygenic scores and breast cancer status in All of Us. Twelve proteins achieved Bonferroni significance in the cross-ancestry meta-analysis (P < 0.05/1,971 tests), including eight previously reported proteins and four newly prioritized by MR. DNPH1 showed cross-ancestry heterogeneity, while CASP8, RALB, and USP28 showed cross-subtype heterogeneity after accounting for shared controls (all P < 0.05/12). Complementary support varied: six candidates showed strong colocalization (PPH4 ≥ 0.80); four replicated with a consistent direction and nominal significance in deCODE, two in the Japan COVID-19 Task Force, and four in All of Us (all P < 0.05). The strongest cumulative support was observed for LRRC25, PARK7, and LRRC37A2. These findings prioritize circulating protein candidates for mechanistic, prevention-oriented, and translational follow-up in breast cancer, while underscoring the need for larger ancestrally diverse proteomic resources to support equitable target and biomarker discovery.

title: Probing a drug-drug based co-crystallization approach to study its impact on solubility, anti-leishmanial and anti-viral activities of Amphotericin B
abstract: Background Leishmaniasis continues to pose a major growing global public health challenge including Pakistan and Yemen. AmB is the standard drug for the treatment with limited clinical utility due to extremely low aqueous solubility, nephrotoxicity, and high cost. Therefore, alternative but equally effective formulation remains a pressing concern. Method In the present study, drug-drug co-crystallization approach successfully employed to modulate the physicochemical and biological properties of AmB without altering its molecular framework. Four new AmB co-crystals (2-5) were synthesized with FDA approved drugs as coformers. Results All co-crystals revealed significant enhancement in solubility, showed potent anti-leishmanial potential against promastigotes of L. donovani except co-crystal 5 as well as anti-viral potential against SARS-CoV-2. major infected murine macrophage cellular assay and the AFM analysis further revealed the promising inhibitory potential against the L. major amastigotes as well. The synthesized co-crystals also showed significantly improved toxicity profiles in comparison to Amphotericin B. Conclusion The initial promising results of the improved anti-leishmanial, potential demonstrated that drug-drug based pharmaceutical co-crystallization may be a promising strategy for improving the therapeutic performance of AmB and therefore, worth to be explored further via detailed in vivo and pharmacokinetic studies.

title: A dimensionless framework for epidemic management: Linking behavioural adaptation to hospital demand
abstract: Abstract This work presents a methodological framework for epidemic management rather than a pathogen-specific model. The COVID-19 pandemic provides an opportunity to calibrate and test the approach across diverse regions and waves. We propose an analytical framework that links behavioural responses to hospital demand. At its core is a single behavioural parameter that captures how populations reduce contacts during outbreaks. Using data from multiple COVID-19 waves across different regions, we show that this parameter reflects age structure and socioeconomic conditions. The framework reveals that stronger behavioural responses consistently reduce peak hospitalisations. The scaling relation is validated against empirical data from 50 US jurisdictions, capturing a substantial component of the observed variation in peak hospitalisation burden. The resulting dimensionless control operator quantifies the reduction in peak demand under non-pharmaceutical interventions, independent of absolute regional capacity. This establishes a unified, parameterisable tool for rapid healthcare forecasting across current and future respiratory pathogens.

title: Vacinas de MRNA e resposta imunológica: mecanismos de ação e eficácia imunológica
abstract: Messenger RNA (MRNA)-based vaccines represent an unprecedented technological revolution in the history of immunology and modern biotechnology, becoming firmly established during the global health crisis triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic. Unlike traditional vaccines, which use attenuated or inactivated pathogens, this innovative platform employs synthetic nucleotide sequences encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles to instruct the host cell machinery to synthesize specific antigens endogenously. This study aimed to conduct an in-depth analysis of the molecular and cellular mechanisms of action of mRNA vaccines, as well as to evaluate their overall immunological efficacy, safety profile, and future therapeutic implications. To this end, a descriptive and analytical integrative literature review was conducted, based on a systematic search of internationally recognized scientific databases, including PubMed, SciELO, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, covering publications from 2019 to 2024. The findings synthesized from the literature demonstrate that MRNA formulations trigger a vigorous and coordinated activation of both innate and adaptive immunity. The internalization of lipid nanoparticles by dendritic cells and macrophages activates pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), inducing the secretion of essential inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Subsequently, antigen presentation via major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules stimulates the activation of helper T lymphocytes (CD4+) and cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CD8+), alongside the maturation of plasma cells that produce high-affinity neutralizing antibodies and the robust generation of long-lived memory T and B lymphocytes. Documented clinical efficacy exceeded 90% against severe symptomatic disease, highlighting the platform's advantages in terms of structural flexibility and rapid adaptability to the continuous emergence of new viral variants. It is concluded that MRNA vaccines extend beyond the scope of COVID-19 prophylaxis, ushering in a new therapeutic era with potential applications in the management of malignant neoplasms, autoimmune diseases, and chronic viral infections.

title: From evidence to decisions: building knowledge translation for pandemic preparedness and response.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic showed that moving evidence quickly into decisions matters as much as strong surveillance, especially in low- and middle-income countries. During the fifteenth session of the WHO Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence Innovation Forum, held on 24 February 2026, speakers from the World Health Organization, the Caribbean Centre for Health Systems Research and Development in Trinidad and Tobago, the United States International University-Africa in Kenya and the Ethiopian Public Health Institute discussed how evidence-to-decision processes are being built and how they perform during health emergencies. The Ethiopian Public Health Institute reported that a dedicated knowledge translation team within the emergency management system reduced the time between a decision maker's question and an evidence response from days or months to hours, drawing on a mandate and relationships established long before the pandemic. In Trinidad and Tobago, a proposed rapid response service could not be established without government funding and engagement, and the momentum gained during COVID-19 faded as the urgency passed. Speakers described arrangements that help sustain evidence use, including the WHO Evidence-informed Policy Network and its six domains of institutionalisation, county-level taskforces, reverse research days and national research agendas. Political turnover, limited resources, unharmonised tools and declining trust in science were identified as the main obstacles. Artificial intelligence was seen as a way to accelerate evidence synthesis, but not to replace the relationships and dialogue at the core of knowledge translation. Moving forward, evidence systems need to be built in ordinary times so that they can support decisions when the next crisis comes.

title: Molecular basis of ACE2 inhibition by the peptide DX600 revealed by computational and biophysical analysis.
abstract: This study investigates the molecular mechanism of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme 2 (ACE2) inhibition by the peptide DX600 using an integrated computational and biophysical approach. Small molecules and peptides have been explored as ACE2 antagonists, including MLN-4760 and the peptide DX600, but the molecular determinants underlying their inhibitory mechanisms remain incompletely understood. MLN-4760 is known to interact within the catalytic cleft of ACE2 thereby inducing structural changes in ACE2 causing the receptor to undergo a transition from opened to closed conformation. On the contrary, our molecular dynamics simulations reveal that DX600 binding stabilizes the receptor, dampening fluctuations of key residues such as to lock the receptor in an open conformation. This stabilization produces a more rigid ACE2 structure, consistent with steric hindrance that may impede viral protein, for example, the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, engagement. RMSF analysis, which quantifies local structural fluctuations at the residue level, confirms that DX600 reduces local residue mobility, highlighting a distinct mechanism from small-molecule inhibitors. These results provide a detailed molecular picture of peptide-mediated ACE2 inhibition and offer insights for the rational design of ACE2-targeted small molecule therapeutics.

title: Federated, Accessible, Inclusive, and Responsive Virtual Biorepository: Delphi Consensus Study.
abstract: Abstract Background The reemergence of the Zika virus, the novel coronavirus, and new influenza strains highlighted the urgent need for an organized forum to access specimens to advance research, diagnostics, and vaccine development. During the COVID-19 pandemic, gaps in supply chains, communication, and standards between local (federated) and centralized systems cost time and lives. The FAIR-VBS (Federated, Accessible, Inclusive, and Responsive Virtual Biorepository) was proposed to connect communities with samples, address specimen-sharing challenges, and promote inclusion and equity. Objective This study aims to enable equitable contribution, sharing, and access to specimens while addressing the complexities involved. The objective is to build stakeholder consensus on prioritized actions, tools, and responsibilities to establish a functional and practical FAIR-VBS. Methods A Delphi process was conducted online to gather stakeholder input and develop a prioritized action plan for the FAIR-VBS. Respondents were recruited using snowball sampling, and questions were informed by participatory workshops, feedback, outreach efforts, and discussions to identify gaps and best practices. The Delphi process consisted of 2 rounds: an initial ranking informed by stakeholder input and a second round to refine priorities based on the panel feedback. Items were evaluated using a standardized 5-point Likert scale and retained if prioritized by at least 70% of respondents rating an item 4 or higher and no more than 15% rating an item below 2, with descriptive statistics applied. Advisory board discussions supplemented the virtual process to capture nuances, while qualitative data were analyzed using participatory action research methods. Results The Delphi process evaluated 34 cumulative items across 2 rounds to identify critical gaps and priorities in biorepository systems. In the first round, 22 out of 30 initial items successfully reached consensus. Panelists organically proposed 4 additional items during the first round; upon evaluation in the second round, 2 of these newly proposed items reached consensus, addressing benefit-sharing challenges (11/15, 73%) and the prioritization of whole blood, plasma, and serum samples (40/42, 95%). Culturally, peripheral blood mononuclear cells were supported as a secondary priority (13/18, 72%). In total, 24 items achieved consensus across both rounds, while 10 items overall did not. Respondents overwhelmingly supported the hybrid FAIR-VBS, which combines federated and centralized systems, offering local convenience with virtual oversight (34/41, 83%). Cost recovery for services was supported by all respondents (43/43, 100%), with a preference for a sliding fee scale to subsidize capacity building in low- and middle-income countries (40/42, 95%). Conclusions Respondents strongly supported the FAIR-VBS to enable equitable access to specimens, services, and benefits. They emphasized the need for clarity on benefit-sharing, regulatory, and ethical frameworks to ensure effective implementation and global inclusivity. A fair and equivalent system to enhance participation and operational continuity is being discussed.

title: Changing Spectrum of Pediatric Liver Diseases: A Single-Center Retrospective Analysis of 423 Cases with Light and Electron Microscopic Findings
abstract: Abstract Background To retrospectively analyze the clinical and pathological characteristics of pediatric liver diseases treated at Beijing Children’s Hospital over the past 9 years, summarize the primary features and evolutionary trends of its disease spectrum, and evaluate the diagnostic value of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for precision diagnosis of pediatric liver disorders. Methods We retrospectively reviewed the clinical data of 423 patients aged ≤ 18 years who presented with liver disease (excluding hepatic tumors) as the primary complaint and underwent successful liver biopsy at Beijing Children's Hospital, Capital Medical University, between January 2017 and December 2025. All biopsy specimens were of adequate quality for paraffin histological and ultrastructural preparation and interpretation. Patients who underwent two biopsies (n = 10) were analyzed separately. Considering the duration of the COVID-19 pandemic and the distribution of samples, the 413 patients with a single biopsy were chronologically divided into three periods—P1 (2017–2019), P2 (2020–2022), and P3 (2023–2025)—and the histopathological types and corresponding disease spectra were compared across the three periods. Results The male-to-female ratio was 1.694:1; the mean age was 7.7 years and the median age was 8.2 years. The three leading diagnostic categories were metabolic liver disease, cholestatic liver disease, and hepatocellular injury. The disease spectrum shifted markedly from P1 to P3, with biopsy numbers rising steadily across periods and the spectrum evolving from a "traditional" pattern dominated by metabolic and cholestatic liver diseases in P1 to a "diversified" pattern in P2–P3, characterized by a relatively balanced distribution of metabolic disease, hepatocellular injury, cholestatic disease, and drug-induced liver injury. Electron microscopy was performed in all 423 children and contributed to the final diagnosis in 286 (67.6%), using a predefined definition of diagnostic contribution. Conclusions The spectrum of pediatric liver diseases changed significantly from P1 to P3, with increasing diversity of disease entities and increasingly refined diagnosis. TEM remains indispensable for the differential diagnosis of genetic-metabolic and infectious subclasses of liver disease, and its application is essential for achieving precise diagnosis and treatment of pediatric liver diseases.

title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design. Design Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023. Setting Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital. Patients One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo. Interventions Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution. Measurements and main results Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods.For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0-6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0-4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed. Conclusions This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

title: Prolonged length of stay in the Italian emergency departments: A competing risks frailty model.
abstract: Background Emergency department (ED) overcrowding has increased worldwide in recent years. This paper provides quantitative information based on data collected immediately before the COVID-19 outbreak, which can serve as a baseline for developing systematic approaches to prolonged length of stay (LoS) in EDs. Materials and methods We analysed a random sample of 10,077 ED accesses drawn from the 503,797 eligible accesses recorded in 2019 in the 16 largest hospitals of Sicily, Italy. LoS was modelled using a cause-specific competing-risks Cox frailty model with Discharge and Hospitalization as competing endpoints. Two log-normal frailty components were included to account for unobserved heterogeneity between EDs and between patients. Non-proportionality was addressed by stratifying on pathology and by including time-varying effects for triage. Cumulative incidence functions (CIFs) were computed to estimate the probability of each endpoint and strata over time. Results Median LoS was 1.70 hours for Discharge and 3.77 hours for Hospitalization, and the gap widened markedly in the upper tail (90th percentile: 7.10 vs 34.95 hours). Discharge was associated with pathology, age, triage, sex and season; Hospitalization with pathology, age, triage and season. The hazard of Discharge decreased by 2% per additional year of age (HR = 0.98, 95% CI 0.977-0.983) and was 10% higher for accesses in summer (HR = 1.10, 95% CI 1.03-1.16). The hazard of Hospitalization increased by 0.4% per year of age (HR = 1.004, 95% CI 1.001-1.007). The effect of triage was time-dependent: at 10 hours of LoS, red-coded accesses had a 69% lower hazard of Discharge (HR = 0.31) and a 53% higher hazard of Hospitalization (HR = 1.53) than other codes. Circulatory and respiratory diseases and blood diseases showed the highest CIFs for Hospitalization and prolonged LoS for both endpoints, whereas skin and musculoskeletal diseases, injuries and poisoning, and nervous system diseases showed the highest CIFs for Discharge. Conclusions Prolonged LoS in Sicilian EDs was driven mainly by pathology, and the exit process differed systematically across disease groups: patients with circulatory and respiratory diseases and with blood diseases waited longest before both Discharge and Hospitalization.The large between-ED heterogeneity in the hazard of Hospitalization, indicates that admission delays reflect organisational as well as structural constraints. Interventions to reduce overcrowding - in particular any expansion of inpatient capacity - should therefore be targeted at the specific wards receiving these patients, rather than applied uniformly across the hospital.

title: Vaccination Among Patients Undergoing Treatment with Janus Kinase Inhibitors: Coverage and Associated Factors
abstract: Background and Objectives: Patients treated with Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) are at increased risk of infections that can be prevented through vaccination. This study evaluated vaccination coverage and associated factors among such patients. Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional study was carried out in the Zaragoza III Healthcare Sector. People receiving JAKi treatment in 2024 were selected. Variables were obtained by reviewing records. Associations with pneumococcal, shingles, 2024–2025 influenza and COVID-19 vaccination were analyzed using bivariate analysis and multiple logistic regression models. Results: A total of 347 patients were analyzed; 64.8% were women with a mean age of 50.8 years. For the 2024–2025 season, influenza vaccination coverage was 51.3%, and COVID-19 vaccination rate was 33.7%. Vaccination coverage against pneumococcal disease and shingles was 76.7% and 73.8%, respectively. Variables associated with having received the four vaccines were being 60 years of age or older (aOR: 2.74; 95% CI: 1.42–5.31), having received the influenza vaccine (aOR: 6.7; 95% CI: 2.85–15.63) and the COVID-19 vaccine (aOR: 4.4; 95% CI: 2.19–8.88) in the previous season, and having been seen at the Preventive Medicine Department Vaccination Clinic (aOR: 9.60; 95% CI: 2.96–31.18). Conclusions: Vaccination rates vary by vaccine, with coverage for influenza and COVID-19 leaving significant room for improvement. Understanding vaccination rates and their associated factors enables the design of specific strategies to improve vaccination coverage. In these strategies, the Preventive Medicine Department Vaccination Clinics can play an important role.

title: Elucidating Bat SuperImmunity: Insights from the Bent-Wing Bat Genome Assembly and Multi-Omics Analysis
abstract: Bats have evolved a range of unique adaptations, including powered flight, echolocation, and exceptional longevity. They have also attracted considerable scientific attention, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic, due to their association with a broad diversity of viruses and their potential role in zoonotic transmission and emerging infectious diseases. Despite hosting numerous viruses, bats often exhibit limited clinical manifestations of infection, suggesting the evolution of distinctive mechanisms of immune regulation and tolerance. Understanding the molecular basis of these mechanisms has become a major focus of current research, with genome-wide analyses providing important insights into the genetic adaptations underlying bat immunity. Nevertheless, the regulatory complexity of bat genomes, particularly the contribution of non-coding RNAs and post-transcriptional RNA editing, remains comparatively underexplored. Here, we present an integrated multi-omic framework for the common bent-wing bat (Miniopterus schreibersii), combining a contiguous chromosome-scale genome assembly with multi-tissue transcriptomic profiling, long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) identification and synteny analysis, endogenous viral elements (EVE) mapping, and same-individual RNA editomic analyses. This study provides a comprehensive resource for investigating genome organization, transcriptional regulation, evolutionary relationships, and post-transcriptional modifications in this species. In particular, it offers an opportunity to explore the potential contribution of non-coding regulatory elements and RNA editing to the molecular mechanisms underlying viral interactions and immune regulation in bats. Collectively, these resources provide a valuable foundation for advancing our understanding of bat genome evolution and the regulatory mechanisms potentially associated with their distinctive responses to viral infections.

title: Long-Term Impact of the BNT162b2 mRNA Vaccine on Graft Function in Lung Transplant Recipients: A Single-Center Retrospective Study
abstract: Background: BNT162b2 vaccination is considered safe in the general population and in solid organ transplant recipients. However, concerns persist that it may induce donor-specific antibodies (DSAs) and trigger rejection in lung transplant recipients (LTRs), and long-term data are limited. This study evaluates the impact of BNT162b2 vaccination on graft function in LTRs. title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
abstract: Nanopore sequencers produce reads within minutes, but metagenomic analysis remains challenging where internet access is limited, data are sensitive or computing resources are modest. EMtrace is an offline pipeline that runs on a laptop during sequencing: it classifies MinKNOW reads, estimates taxon abundance by expectation-maximization (EM) and assembles reference-based consensus genomes. We benchmarked it against five virome and four 16S rRNA tools on simulated, mock-community and clinical data. On field isolates and 16 SARS-CoV-2 clinical samples, EMtrace had the highest species-level F1 score (1.00 and 0.97) and one false-positive species, against 3-7 for the comparators. It recovered divergent viruses as completely as ViMOP, and low-titre field libraries more completely, at ≥99.7% identity. In replayed runs, it identified the target virus in the first 4,000-read batch (5-13 min). With a shared 16S reference, EMtrace reported two to three times fewer false-positive species than Emu.

title: Hyaluronic acid based codelivery vaccine enhances humoral immunity through active lymph node targeting.
abstract: Efficient co-delivery of antigens and adjuvants to secondary lymphoid organs represents a pivotal challenge in subunit vaccine development, aiming to enhance immunogenicity while minimizing systemic side effects. Although various nanocarrier systems have been explored for lymphatic targeting, many rely on passive drainage or non-specific cellular uptake, lacking active targeting mechanisms for efficient lymph nodes (LNs) accumulation. Here, we constructed a lymph node targeting vaccine by covalently conjugating the SARS-CoV-2 S1 subunit and the TLR7/8 agonist 3 M-052 onto a hyaluronic acid (HA) scaffold, termed HA-3 M-052-S1. We systematically evaluated its binding to the lymphatic endothelial receptor LYVE-1, lymph node targeting efficiency, and immunogenicity in mice. Our results demonstrate that HA-3 M-052-S1 exhibited high-affinity binding to LYVE-1 and rapidly accumulated in draining lymph nodes (dLNs) within 4 h post-injection. The vaccine induced significantly higher frequencies of T follicular helper cells and germinal center B cells compared to alum-adjuvanted or simple mixture formulations. Moreover, it elicited potent and durable antigen-specific antibody responses, with neutralizing antibody titers substantially exceeding those of control groups. Importantly, the co-crosslinked vaccine conferred protection against SARS-CoV-2 challenge comparable to an adenoviral vector vaccine. This study establishes an active lymph node targeting strategy via HA-LYVE-1 interaction and provides a robust platform for next-generation subunit vaccines with enhanced potency and safety.

title: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus
abstract: Human coronaviruses (HCoVs) range from mild seasonal strains to pathogenic viruses that cause severe pneumonia. The virological and host determinants that distinguish pathogenic coronaviruses (MERS‐CoV, SARS‐CoV‐2) from seasonal strains (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-OC43) remain poorly defined. To identify determinants of pathogenicity, we systematically compared replication, cellular tropism, innate responses and cytopathogenicity of pathogenic compared with seasonal HCoVs across nasal, bronchial, small airway and embryonic stem cell derived alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cell cultures. All HCoVs preferentially infected ciliated cells in the upper airway, but only pathogenic viruses replicated to high titres in AT2 cells. Pathogenic HCoVs reprogrammed AT2 function and suppressed key innate immune signatures, consistent with distal lung epithelial dysfunction. In contrast, seasonal HCoVs were associated with limited alveolar replication and milder disruption of AT2 homeostasis. Strikingly, despite modest replication in all cell types, HCoV-229E induced pronounced epithelial injury, cilia loss and strong interferon stimulated gene expression, as well as induction of cellular stress/death programmes resembling those induced by MERS-CoV. These findings highlight the striking differences in cellular responses throughout the airways and between distinct HCoV strains and emphasizes the importance of assessing distal lung tropism and epithelial host responses to evaluate emergent coronaviruses to inform pandemic preparedness strategies.

title: Antibody design across observed and forecasted antigenic evolution
abstract: The therapeutic efficacy of antibodies is often limited by the evolution of their targets. Designing or eliciting antibodies that withstand such evolution is challenging as their binding interfaces must accommodate antigenic variation. Here, we introduce Germinal Multi, a computational framework for de novo antibody design and rescue that jointly optimizes a single paratope against multiple antigenic variants. We applied Germinal Multi to cancer and viral antigens, targeting both observed antigenic variation and prospective antibody escape. Multi-target optimization yielded antibodies that bound resistance-associated EGFR variants or that neutralized antigenically distinct historical SARS-CoV-2 variants, with recognition extending to variants withheld from the design process. Beyond acting on observed evolution, we redesigned the broadly neutralizing antibody BD55-1205 to restore neutralization of a prospective escape variant engineered with guidance from an evolutionary forecasting model, while preserving activity against the parental variant. Successful candidates were identified after screening tens of designs per campaign. Together, these results establish multi-target computational design as a strategy for generating antibody breadth across observed antigenic variation and demonstrate the potential of evolutionary forecasting to guide antibody redesign against prospective escape.

title: Progress and Polarization: A Chronological Review of Vaccine Innovation and Mistrust
abstract: Background/Objectives: Vaccination has dramatically reduced the burden of infectious disease, yet public trust in vaccines has fluctuated throughout history. This review examines the historical relationship between vaccine innovation and public confidence. Methods: A chronological narrative review of peer-reviewed historical and public health literature was conducted, organized into four eras spanning early variolation through the COVID-19 pandemic. Cross-era synthesis identified recurring themes influencing vaccine acceptance and trust. Results: Across the literature reviewed, vaccine confidence moved through recurring cycles of innovation, acceptance, disruption, and adaptation, and public responses varied across countries and social groups. Although scientific advances improved vaccine safety and effectiveness, public trust was consistently shaped by broader social, political, cultural, and communication factors. Major events—including the introduction of germ theory, the Cutter Incident, the Wakefield controversy, and the COVID-19 pandemic—served as turning points in public perceptions of vaccination. Conclusions: Scientific advancement alone has never guaranteed public trust. Understanding vaccine hesitancy as a historically recurring phenomenon may inform more effective public health strategies that emphasize transparency, institutional credibility, and community engagement alongside continued scientific innovation.

title: Lagged environmental effects on multi-pathogen respiratory positivity: a distributed-lag nonlinear analysis of seven Sichuan sentinel hospitals, China
abstract: Abstract Acute respiratory infections (ARI) impose a large global burden and show marked seasonality that implicates environmental drivers, yet the lagged effects of these exposures on pathogen-specific positivity remain poorly characterised. Using case-level data from seven sentinel hospitals in Sichuan, China (2024–2026) aggregated to a weekly panel of 23 014 ARI cases, we applied quasi-Poisson distributed-lag non-linear models (cross-basis, 6-week lag; trend spline; city effects; log offset) to estimate cumulative relative risks (90th versus 10th percentile) for temperature, relative humidity and six air pollutants, with within-pathogen false-discovery-rate control. At least one pathogen was detected in 51.9% of cases and co-detection in 18.2%; Haemophilus influenzae and influenza predominated. Relative humidity gave the most stable single-exposure association with respiratory syncytial virus positivity ( RR 2.01, 95% CI 1.06–3.82); it failed FDR control (adjusted P = 0.130 ) and was nullified by temperature co-adjustment ( RR 1.05). influenzae rose with temperature and ozone and fell with PM2.5; SARS-CoV-2 tracked carbon monoxide. Twelve of 40 estimates survived FDR control. The humidity–RSV signal is robust to model specification yet fragile under co-varying exposures — the cautionary lesson — and the reusable output is a transparent screening framework that exposes such fragility, serving exposure science and environmental epidemiology.

title: Contrasting pre- and post-COVID changes in within-host gp60 diversity among human-infecting Cryptosporidium species.
abstract: Population connectivity influences genetic diversity by facilitating exchange among populations. For enteric parasites, connectivity depends on host contact and environmentally mediated transmission, suggesting that disruptions to human movement could reduce diversity within infections. The COVID-19 pandemic provided a natural experiment to test this prediction. We used high-throughput gp60 metabarcoding to compare within-host amplicon sequence variant (ASVs) richness, diversity and composition before and after the pandemic in three human-infecting Cryptosporidium species with contrasting transmission ecologies: anthroponotic Cryptosporidium hominis , zoonotic Cryptosporidium parvum and wildlife-associated Cryptosporidium cuniculus . Primary analyses excluded 26 epidemiologically linked C. hominis infections from a 2023 outbreak; sensitivity analyses included these samples. hominis showed significantly lower Shannon, Simpson and inverse-Simpson diversity, 63% fewer detectable ASVs and altered ASV composition. Cryptosporidium parvum showed compositional differences but no significant reduction in diversity or richness, whereas C. cuniculus showed no clear temporal change. Including outbreak-associated C. hominis samples attenuated diversity reductions but retained significant declines in Shannon diversity, Simpson diversity, ASV richness and composition. These findings are consistent with reduced parasite connectivity following disruption of predominantly human-associated transmission and indicate that major changes in transmission conditions can rapidly reshape the genetic diversity maintained within parasite infections.

title: The role of dental public health in patient, public and the professions' safety: insights and case studies from England.
abstract: Introduction Dental public health (DPH) is a clinical dental specialty that works across six domains and the three pillars of public health, including health protection. Across the UK, the DPH speciality workforce plays a vital role in the management of dental health protection cases, utilising their system-level knowledge and clinical leadership to address complex health protection incidents in dental setting. This paper is one of two papers dealing with health protection as part of this Themed Issue on the speciality and aims to provide insights to the systems leadership role it plays within health protection across the UK. The second paper is focussed on antimicrobial resistance, which is another key element of protecting the health of our population.Methods This paper provides a narrative overview of the role of dental public health and includes case studies focussed on the contribution of specialist leadership during the COVID-19 pandemic response and the management of a dental case involving a practice with infection prevention control concerns.Case studies Through these case studies, the proactive and wide impact the speciality has in the protection of patients, the public and the dental workforce is highlighted.Conclusions The management of complex dental incidents, with health protection concerns requires robust, timely, and evidence-informed system response. Specialists in DPH provide critical clinical and system leadership, enabling partnership working and influencing coordinated actions across organisational boundaries. Their specialist understanding of the unique combination of dentistry and public health is crucial for patients, public, and healthcare workforce protection.
